activity: professional tone, structured writing and respectful disagreement in formal communication
knowledge_domain: professional tone, structured writing and respectful disagreement in formal communication
fact: A 2005 study by Justin Kruger, Nicholas Epley and colleagues found that email writers overestimate how well readers will pick up their intended tone, such as sarcasm or seriousness.
story:
The reply arrived at 11:52 p.m., which was the first sign that something had gone wrong. Mr. Mwangi never wrote at night. Sofia read the two lines twice on her phone, elbow propped on the kitchen counter: "Sofia, I was disappointed by the tone of your message. Please come see me before class." She scrolled up to her own email, the one she had sent that afternoon about her extended essay on the Panama Canal, the one that ended with, "Well, at least now I know why it took ten years, ha." At the time it had felt light, the kind of thing she would say laughing in his classroom. On the screen, in the gray thread, it sat there like a splinter.

She called Leonie, who was still awake because Leonie was always still awake. "Read it to me again," Leonie said, so Sofia read the whole thread aloud, her voice going flat and formal in a way she hadn't noticed when she wrote it. "Okay," Leonie said, "honestly, without knowing you, that last line sounds kind of sarcastic. Like you're mocking the assignment." "I wasn't mocking anything. I was mocking myself. There's a difference." "Sure," Leonie said, "to you."

Sofia opened her laptop and typed a reply, then deleted it, then typed another: "I'm sorry the email came across that way. That was not my intention." She stopped. Intention, she thought, was doing a lot of work in that sentence, as if the words had traveled safely and simply been misdelivered, rather than having left her hands already changed. Robert had shown her something in the library two weeks ago, a printout he kept folded in his binder like contraband. "Listen to this," he had said, tapping the page. "A 2005 study by Kruger, Epley, and a bunch of other people. Email writers overestimate how well readers will pick up their intended tone. Sarcasm, seriousness, all of it." "That's a study?" Sofia had said. "Somebody got funded for that?" Robert had shrugged. "Somebody had to be right about it."

She remembered the moment now with a small, melancholic weight, because she had laughed at the printout, and here she was living inside it. The joke about the canal had seemed safe because she could hear it, could hear her own voice pitching up on the ha, could see her own shrug. But the message that arrived in Mr. Mwangi's inbox arrived voiceless, and the voice he supplied for it was evidently not hers. Robert's paper had said the writers believed, on average, that their tone would come through about three-quarters of the time, which meant that whatever confidence she had felt pressing send was itself the error, not a fact about the message.

At seven forty the next morning she stood outside the humanities office, holding a printed copy of the thread with her annotations in the margins. Through the door she could hear him on the phone with the exam board, his voice patient and clipped, and she rehearsed her opening line under her breath. When he hung up and waved her in, she laid the pages on his desk. "I wanted to show you how I read my own email," she said. "The joke was aimed at me, at how slowly I work. I've marked where I thought it would land."

Mr. Mwangi put on his glasses and read. He was quiet long enough that she studied the canal diagram tacked above his filing cabinet, the isthmus rendered in blue ballpoint, the narrow neck of land the whole essay had been about, the thing that made the canal both possible and necessary. "All right," he said finally. "I misread that." Then he pushed the pages back toward her. "But notice what it cost you to fix. A meeting, a printout, a morning. A joke in person is free. A joke in writing is a loan against the reader's generosity." She wrote that down before she could decide whether she agreed with it.

"Mr. Mwangi," she said, closing her notebook, "I'm going to rewrite the whole correspondence section of my research log. Structure it properly. But I still think the problem isn't that jokes don't belong in email. It's that the writer gets to hear the joke and the reader doesn't, so the reader has to invent one, and the invented one is usually worse. That's not a rule about email. That's just bad luck for the reader." He looked at her over the glasses. "You could also say it's bad luck for the writer, since the writer is the one standing in my office at seven forty in the morning."

On the walk to first period she passed Leonie at the lockers and told her, briefly, that it had gone fine, that it had actually gone better than fine, that the essay deadline had been extended for everyone because of the confusion. Leonie said, "So you were rewarded for being misunderstood," and Sofia stopped in the corridor, her bag strap twisted under her hand, because that wasn't the version she had been carrying in her head, and she could not immediately find the sentence that would make both versions true. Behind them the bell rang, and the hallway began to extrude its slow current of students toward the science wing. "Write me an email about it," Leonie said, pulling open the door. "I promise I'll read it in the right tone."

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: Elgar took the title Pomp and Circumstance from Shakespeare's Othello, which mentions the "pride, pomp, and circumstance of glorious war."
story:
Austin arrived at Tiger's backyard with his gown still hanging in the car, folded over the passenger seat like a shed skin. The ceremony had run long, the principal had mispronounced four names, and the brass quartet had played the same eight bars of Elgar until Austin thought he might never hear anything else. Now Tiger's father was burning chicken on the grill and someone's little sister was selling cups of lemonade at a card table, an operation that struck Austin as the embryonic stage of the oligarchy that would one day own the neighborhood.

Austin's problem was simpler than economics and harder than most of his exams: Jessica was leaving for Portugal in nine days, and he had decided, somewhere during the handshake on the stage, that he would tell her before the party ended that he had liked her since junior year. He had a plastic cup of punch and a plan with no words in it yet.

Tiger had other priorities. Tiger had spent the year taking one English elective, Mr. Almeida's class, and had emerged with the conviction that this qualified him to pontificate about literature at any gathering, including this one. He stood on the low retaining wall near the fence and held forth about the tragedy they had studied in the spring.

"The whole play is about what a man can't say out loud," Tiger announced. "Othello. Iago twists everything because nobody just says the thing."

"The play is about jealousy," said a cousin of Tiger's, through a mouthful of chips.

"Sure," said Tiger, "and the moon is about cheese."

Austin was only half listening. The band had played Elgar twice more in the ceremony, once while the seniors filed in and once, absurdly, over the loudspeakers while the photographer reset his tripod. Something about the march snagged in his mind now, and he did what he always did with a snag: he worried it in front of people until it gave.

"Who named it," he said. "The march. Pomp and Circumstance. Somebody chose that."

"Elgar chose it," said Mr. Almeida, who had appeared at the table of chips in his shirtsleeves, holding a cup and looking like a man who had graded his last essay of the year and intended to grade no one's anything until September. "But he lifted it."

"Lifted it where?" Austin asked.

Mr. Almeida only raised his cup and drifted toward the grill, which was the teacher's version of find out yourself. Tiger looked personally wounded that a fact had entered his territory uninvited. He pulled out his phone, typed, and went quiet in a way that meant the internet had contradicted no one yet.

Austin turned it over while Jessica came over to the wall with her own punch. He remembered the spring, the classroom smelling of rain, Mr. Almeida reading the speech where Othello strips himself of everything. He had liked the play more than he had admitted, and he heard the line before he could place it, the pride, the pomp, and the circumstance of glorious war. That was it. Elgar had taken his title straight out of Othello, out of the speech where a soldier says goodbye to his whole occupation.

"Elgar took the title Pomp and Circumstance from Othello," Austin said. "Pride, pomp, and circumstance of glorious war. We read it in April."

"You're making that up," said Tiger, but his phone had just finished loading and he read the screen twice, and his face did the thing a pontificate's face does when the pulpit is pulled out from under it. "Huh," Tiger said. "Okay. That's actually good."

Jessica looked at Austin with her head tipped slightly, the way she looked at a proof in margin notes. "So we walked in to a song named after a man losing everything he was good at."

"That's one way to start a graduation," Austin said.

"Or the honest way," she said.

Tiger's cousin asked whether Elgar was on the test. Mr. Almeida, from the grill, said that everything was on the test, and the whole year had been the test, and then he asked Tiger's father whether the chicken was supposed to be that color, which started a small war of its own at the fence.

The party thinned toward dark. Austin helped stack chairs and found himself next to Jessica by the lemonade table, where the little sister was counting her earnings under a porch light. Nine days. He had the fact about Elgar now, which was not the thing he had come here to say, but which had come out of him first, easily, because facts were easy.

"Portugal," he said. "Nine days."

"Eight and a half," Jessica said. She folded the last napkin in the stack and put it under the weight so the wind wouldn't take it. "You going to say the other thing, or do I have to stand here through the cleanup?"

The porch light buzzed. Down the yard, Tiger was telling his cousin that the play was about what a man can't say out loud, with more feeling now, as if he had invented the idea on the walk over.

"I liked you since junior year," Austin said. "I'm not sure what to do with that now. But there it is."

Jessica picked up the cup of punch she had set on the table, considered it, and handed it to him to hold.

"Walk me to the car," she said.

activity: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
knowledge_domain: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
fact: In hockey, a saucer pass lifts the puck just off the ice so it flies flat over an opponent's stick and lands on the receiver's blade.
story:
The town floods the baseball diamond every December, boards nailed along the base paths, and by the second week of the new year the infield is ice and the outfield is a sheet of grey water gone solid under the streetlight. Ms. Njoroge, who lives in the house past centre field and pays the water bill nobody else will pay, meets Maya at the gate with the key to the skate shack and a plastic bin of pucks.

The coach is away for two weeks and Maya, who is sixteen, has been given the team in his absence, eight kids between nine and eleven, plus her classmates Maeva and Erin to help herd them. She takes the bin, sets it on the bench, and tells the kids to pass while she watches.

The trouble is not hard to find. In the scrimmage, every pass through the middle dies on the blade of the other team's stick. The smallest kid, a centre with mismatched gloves, tries the same lane four times and four times the puck is knocked away before it arrives. Maya writes in her notebook, pass gets blocked, and underlines it, and does not write the sentence that is actually true, which is that she has no idea what to do about it.

She tries cones first. She spaces them so the passes have to travel wider, around the defenders, and for ten minutes this seems like a plan, and then a defenceman simply reaches further and the play dies again. The small centre skates back to the line with his chin down. Maya had wanted, more than anything, to correct these kids without eviscerating whatever it was that made them want the puck in the first place, and she can see she is close to doing exactly that.

Maeva arrives mid-practice with a thermos and a lot of opinions. "So you're the coach now," she says, which is not a question.

"I'm the one holding the cones," Maya says.

"You're sixteen."

"They're nine. The math works out." Maya says it lightly but her hands are cold in her gloves and she knows Maeva can see the notebook page, which is half a page, and mostly underlined.

"They keep going back to the middle," Erin says from the bench, where she is tying a kid's skate. "Like recidivism."

"They're not criminals," Maeva says.

"They're repeat offenders."

Later, when the kids are shooting at the far boards, Maya stands at the fence with her cold hands in her armpits and watches the older shinny players who share the ice in the evenings, the ones with the good jackets. One of them takes a pass at the blue line with a man's stick flat on the ice in front of him, and instead of forcing it through, he opens his blade and the puck lifts, just barely, clearing the ice, travelling flat through the air, over the laid-out stick, and coming down on his teammate's blade without a bounce. Maya stands very still. She watches until he does it again.

"Maeva," she says. "What is that called?"

"Saucer pass," Maeva says, without looking up from her phone. "My brother does them."

The next drill is simple, which Maya thinks is probably the point of drills. Two lines, fifteen feet apart, and between them Erin lies a broom handle flat on the ice. The pass has to go over the handle and land on the blade on the other side, not in front of it, not behind it. The first few attempts are disasters, pucks skipping sideways, one clearing the boards entirely and rolling off toward the pelagic dark of the frozen outfield, where they will find it in April. Then the small centre steps up, opens his blade the way the man with the good jacket did, and the puck rises, sails flat, and settles onto his linemate's tape.

The kids make a noise like something has been unblocked in the room.

Ms. Njoroge comes down from her porch to watch the last ten minutes, her boots crunching the frozen gravel. She does not coach, which Maya is grateful for. She watches the broom handle drill, and she watches the small centre land three in a row, and then she says, "What happens when the stick moves?"

"I don't know yet," Maya says.

"They'll try it in a game Saturday."

"I know."

Ms. Njoroge nods and turns back up the path. On the ice the small centre takes another turn, and this time he waits, holding the puck while the receiver waves, and then the puck goes up flat over the handle and comes down soft on the tape.

"Again," Maya says. "Line up, we're not done."

activity: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
knowledge_domain: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
fact: In standard notation, vertical bar lines divide the staff into bars, also called measures, and a final double bar line with one thick line marks the end of a piece.
story:
The music room smelled of valve oil and radiator dust, and Sofia had claimed the piano by the window before anyone else could. Her assignment sheet lay flat on the music stand: compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes, written in standard notation, due Friday. Three weeks into the term, Mr. Mokoena had made it sound simple, the way he made everything sound simple, and then he had left the room to deal with a broken timpani, and the simplicity had evaporated the moment Sofia picked up her pencil.

She had the melody in her head. That was the maddening part. It arrived on the walk to school, hummed itself through chemistry, and now sat in her skull refusing to be caught. She could play it, roughly, hunting for the notes on the piano, but when she tried to write it down, the staff paper stared back with its five lines and its small clef like a closed gate.

Julien dropped into the chair beside her with his own sheet, already covered in neat quarter notes. He wanted to finish early, always, because finishing early was his religion; he proselytized about it constantly, urging everyone to stop fiddling and just commit. "Write something, anything," he said now. "Sixteen bars of anything is better than two bars of perfect."

"Two bars of perfect is what I have."

"Then fourteen bars of anything." He slid his page toward her so she could see the vertical lines drawn through his staff, dividing the music into neat boxes. "I counted mine twice. Fifteen, then sixteen. I kept miscounting the last one because of that double thing at the end."

Sofia leaned over. At the far right of Julien's staff stood two bar lines together, the second one noticeably thicker than the first. She had drawn those on her own page without thinking, copying the shape from a piece of sheet music in her folder, the way you copy a signature without reading it.

"That's how you know it's over," said River, arriving with a keyboard under one arm and a granola bar in her teeth. River wanted, above all, to be the person who knew things in this room, and she usually was. "The vertical lines chop the staff into bars. Some people call them measures, same thing. And at the end of the whole piece you put the double one, thick line and thin line, so nobody plays on into the silence."

"Nobody was going to play into the silence," Julien said.

"You'd be surprised. Mr. Mokoena has stories."

Sofia looked back at her own two bars, and something rearranged itself in her thinking. All week she had been treating the melody as one long breath, a river of sound that she would somehow pour onto the page. But the page did not want a river. It wanted compartments. She took a ruler from her pencil case and drew vertical lines through her staff, one after another, and suddenly the empty space was not one terrifying blank but sixteen small rooms, each waiting to be furnished. She played her two bars, wrote them into the first compartment, and then, instead of composing bar seventeen in the air, she asked a smaller question: what belongs in this box? A chord change on the third beat. A note that answers the note before it. The melody, which had been hiding, began to come out as if it had only wanted to be invited properly.

River, who was supposed to be practicing scales, watched over her shoulder for a while. When Sofia faltered at bar nine, River reached past her and played the chord she thought Sofia intended, softly, so that Sofia could hear the disagreement between what was written and what was meant. "Your B flat wants to resolve," River said. "It's been leaning all afternoon."

"It can lean for one more bar. I like the suspense."

"You would," Julien said, but he said it while moving his own chair closer, and when Sofia's eraser shredded a hole in the paper at bar eleven, he was the one who produced a fresh sheet from his bag without being asked. He did not comment on it. He just flattened the crease out with the side of his hand and went back to his own work.

Mr. Mokoena returned with bandages on two fingers and a garrulous account of the timpani's head, which had split, he claimed, out of pure spite, and which had turned his free period into something other than the sinecure he had been promised when he took the job. He circulated through the room, and when he reached Sofia's stand he did not lecture. He tapped the final double bar line she had drawn, the thin and the thick, and raised one eyebrow at her, and she nodded.

At the end of the period Sofia counted her compartments with the ruler's edge, touching each one. Fifteen. She counted again from the thick line backwards, and there it was: she had skipped a bar line somewhere around the repeat of her opening phrase, so that one box held eight beats instead of four. River leaned in, and together they found the missing line, and Sofia drew it in, and the sixteenth room opened up, small and square and empty, waiting.

"Well," River said. "One more to furnish."

activity: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
knowledge_domain: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
fact: Alfred Cobban's 1954 inaugural lecture at University College London, published in 1955 as The Myth of the French Revolution, attacked the Marxist social interpretation.
story:
Jayden had told Danny he practically lived in the city archive, which was true in the sense that he had been there twice and intended to go often. The third visit was today, a Saturday in March, with a legal pad and a pen because Ms. Berg had banned laptops for the outlining stage. She wanted the bones of the argument before the flesh. Jayden wanted the opposite, which was to write something grandiose about liberty and terror and have it done by Sunday night.

The reading room smelled of dust that had been organized. Behind the desk sat Ms. Berg herself, which he had not expected, since she was a teacher and it was Saturday and teachers presumably had houses. She was bent over a card catalogue with the concentration of someone defusing something. Her want, though Jayden did not know it yet, was a promotion to head of department, and she had decided that spending weekends among primary sources would prove something to whoever decided such things.

Danny arrived twenty minutes late carrying two coffees and a folded printout. "Okay, so I did the reading you skipped," Danny said, sliding into the chair across from Jayden. Danny's want was simpler and closer to the surface: he wanted to be the one who had done the reading, and to be seen having done it.

"I didn't skip it," Jayden said. This was not accurate. He had read the first four pages and the conclusion and formed the impression that the rest agreed with them.

"You said the Marxist view was never really challenged, just, like, updated." Danny unfolded the printout and smoothed it flat on the table. "That's not what this says. There's a specific guy. Cobban. Alfred Cobban. 1954, his inaugural lecture at University College London. It got published in 1955 as The Myth of the French Revolution, and it attacked the Marxist social interpretation. That's the moment. That's what you write down when you outline."

Jayden copied the name and the dates onto the legal pad, and something in his chest seemed to palpitate, though he told Danny it was the coffee. The sentences felt different now that they had a hinge. Before Cobban there was one story about why the Revolution happened, and after Cobban there was a fight about the story, and an essay about how views had changed since 1800 needed exactly that fight at its centre. He began drawing arrows between paragraphs. He crossed out his opening line, which he had been privately proud of, about the Revolution being a flame that never dies. "That's a platitude," he admitted, and Danny said he had been going to say that for two days.

Ms. Berg came over on her way to the photocopier and looked at the legal pad upside down. "Cobban," she read. "Good. Whose side are you on?"

"I think Cobban was right," Jayden said, because he had read half a page about him and half a page felt like a lot.

"About what, specifically?"

He looked at the pad. The arrows went both ways. Some went back the way they came. "About the social interpretation being a myth," he said, and then, because her face did not move, "except I haven't read him yet. Only about him. And the other people say the Marxists had a point about the peasants, so maybe it's not a myth so much as an exaggeration, and Cobban knocked it down without building anything, which the other book says, but the other book might be unfair to him." He heard himself and stopped. "I don't know yet. I know the date now. That's something."

"It's more than most of your class will have by Monday," Ms. Berg said, and went back to her cards.

Danny drank his coffee and watched Jayden work for a while. "So you're going with Cobban," he said finally.

"I'm going with 1954," Jayden said. "The rest is still open."

He sat there until the light through the high windows went from white to grey, filling in the outline, leaving gaps where the gaps belonged. When the announcement came that the archive closed at five, he packed the legal pad carefully, the way you carry something unfinished, and Danny held the door. Outside, Ms. Berg was waiting at the bus stop, still holding a drawer of catalogue cards she had apparently been allowed to take home. "You realize," she said, nodding at the cards, "I've spent my whole Saturday in a building full of other people's facts, trying to prove I belong here." Jayden looked at his legal pad, at the arrows pointing in both directions, and said, "At least you know which way yours point."

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Acrylic paint is water-based while wet, but it dries quickly and becomes water-resistant once dry.
story:
The craft shed smelled of pine sap and turpentine substitutes, and by the second week of August it had become Faith's favourite place at camp, mostly because nobody bothered her there. She was building a diorama of the lake at sunset, which Mr. Côté, the crafts director, had approved with a nod so brief she suspected he hadn't looked. That was fine. She preferred it that way. The project was hers: layered cardboard hills, a foil water, and a sky she meant to blend from orange to a deep, layered blue.

The problem was the blue. Every time she mixed it, it dried on her palette before she could feather it into the orange, leaving a hard stripe instead of a soft one. She had started over three times, each hilltop torn off and rebuilt, and the cardboard was getting thin in that corner.

"You're doing it wrong," Karim said from the doorway, holding a popsicle he had no intention of finishing. He was the camp's resident sardonic commentator, the one who narrated the canoe races like a disillusioned sportscaster and kept a running list of staff absurdities in the back of his notebook.

"I'm doing it my way," Faith said, and dipped her brush again.

He settled onto the stool across from her anyway. "Brent says you should just spray it. He saw it in a video. You know Brent. He operationalizes everything. Watches a tutorial, makes a checklist, done."

"Brent built a birdhouse that looks like a parking garage."

"A very straight parking garage." Karim pointed the popsicle stick at her palette, where a ridge of dried blue had already formed along the edge. "Also, you left your brushes out at lunch. Again."

She looked down at her good brush, the thin one, and found it stiff as a twig, the bristles frozen into a bent point. When she tried to bend them back they crackled faintly, and a fine flake of dried blue came off onto her finger. The cheap ones she'd left soaking in her water cup were worse: the water had done nothing at all, and the paint had set around the ferrule like a shell.

"Water's not going to fix that," Karim said, watching her swirl the ruin in the cup. "It's weird. It thins when it's wet, like it's on your side, and then it turns on you." He wasn't being helpful so much as interested, which was his way of being a friend.

Faith carried the stiff brush to the window and held it up to the light. So that was the trick of it: the paint would cooperate with water only while it was still wet, and after that you were on your own. Which meant the stripe in her sky wasn't a failure of mixing. It was a failure of speed. She had been treating the paint like something patient, and it wasn't. She thought of her mother, who had wanted her to take the pre-college maths intensive this summer instead of camp, who said things like "learn what the world actually runs on." Faith had argued that she wanted to make things. But maybe it wasn't either-or. Maybe the sensible thing was to take the paint as it actually behaved, not as she wished it would, and work with its limits the way Brent would, with a plan, without giving up the picture in her head. She wasn't sure that counted as compromise or as sense. She wasn't sure it mattered which it was called.

She mixed a fresh pool of blue, wider than before, and a second pool of orange, and laid out three clean brushes in a row like instruments before a surgery. Then she painted fast, wet into wet, dragging the colours toward each other before either could set. The stripe that had defeated her all week softened into a gradient, orange bleeding up into blue like weather happening.

The sky worked. The brush was still ruined, though, and when she peeled the dried blue off the ferrule, half the bristles came with it. She set the bent little brush on the windowsill, dead and useful, and stood back to look at the whole diorama, its hills and foil water and the new sky above them, all of it due to be judged tomorrow by people who would never know how many versions had come before.

Karim leaned in beside her, popsicle dripping onto the floorboards. "So what are you going to tell Brent?"

"Tell him his birdhouse is a parking garage," Faith said, "and then ask for his checklist."

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The first Super Bowl was played on January 15, 1967, when the Green Bay Packers beat the Kansas City Chiefs 35 to 10 in Los Angeles.
story:
Caleb had never watched a Super Bowl inside an ice rink before, but Ms. Jean-Louis had rigged two televisions above the skate rental counter and declared the party open to anyone with five dollars and a working knowledge of nacho etiquette. The rink itself sat dark and gleaming beyond the glass, unused for the evening, a cold mirror in which the game floated upside down and green.

His grandfather planted himself in the best folding chair an hour before kickoff, wearing a Packers jersey so old the green had gone the color of pond water. "I remember the very first one," he announced to the whole room, to Caleb, to Robin and Kaiden dragging chairs over, to Ms. Jean-Louis counting slices of pizza. "First Super Bowl ever. January 15, 1967. Green Bay played Kansas City and beat them 35 to 10, out in Los Angeles. I watched every minute of it."

"You were alive in 1967?" Kaiden said, dropping into a seat with the ceremonial slowness of someone who has just located a flaw in a bridge. "No offense, Mr. Caleb's grandpa, but that sounds like something you half remember from a cereal box."

"I have a whole brain," the grandfather said, "unlike certain referees I could name."

Caleb did the arithmetic in his head while the pregame show droned. His grandfather was seventy-three, which put him at sixteen or seventeen in January of 1967, which was actually possible, which was somehow stranger than if it had been impossible. Sixteen, the same age Caleb was now, sitting in a room watching a game his grandfather had watched at sixteen. The coincidence felt like a thread waiting to suture two afternoons together, decades apart, and Caleb was not sure he wanted them joined, because if his grandfather's memory was true then it was a kind of inheritance, and if it was false then it was a kind of theater, and both possibilities deserved respect.

Robin, meanwhile, had her own agenda, which was the arcade machine by the vending wall. She had been feeding it quarters since November trying to break the rink's high score, and she kept one eye on the screen of skaters and Packers highlights while her fingers worked the joystick. "I'm going to do it tonight," she said, not looking up. "Distraction is good for me. If I think about it, I fail. If there's a whole Super Bowl happening, I become unstoppable."

"Robin, the game's on," Kaiden said.

"The game is always on," Robin said. "Somewhere."

Caleb leaned toward Kaiden and lowered his voice. "Can you look something up? Don't make it a thing." Kaiden already had his phone out, which for Kaiden was the natural resting position of his hands, and he typed with the smug efficiency of a magistrate delivering a verdict he had drafted in advance.

"He's right," Kaiden said, sounding personally betrayed by his own phone. "First Super Bowl, January 15, 1967. Packers over the Chiefs, 35 to 10, in Los Angeles. It's all right there."

"Wait," Caleb said. "He said he watched it. Where did he watch it?"

This was the part that itched. His grandfather had spent his whole childhood in Ohio, Caleb was fairly sure, on a street he described in suspiciously perfect detail, and Los Angeles was not Ohio. Caleb crossed the folding-chair territory and crouched by the pond-water jersey. "Grandpa. The first one. Where were you when you watched it?"

His grandfather took a slow pull of his soda, savoring the room's attention like a man who had rehearsed this exact pause. "On the couch," he said. "My father's couch. In Cleveland. I never said I was in Los Angeles, I said the game was there. Sixteen years old, and my father let me stay up for the whole thing, which was the miracle." He grinned. "You thought I was lying about being there?"

"Kaiden thought you were lying about everything," Caleb said.

"I thought the whole memory was anachronistic," Kaiden said, with dignity. "I stand by my method. I just got the wrong result."

So both things were true at once, Caleb decided, sitting back down as the second half began. His grandfather had remembered it exactly, every number in the right place, and he had also dressed it up a little, the way you press a suit before wearing it. Caleb filed that under something he could not fully resolve and did not need to, which was a new sensation and not an unpleasant one. The Packers were winning now, which made his grandfather insufferable in a way the whole room seemed to enjoy.

In the fourth quarter, when the score stopped being interesting, Robin finally walked to the arcade machine, cracked her knuckles, and played the best game of her life while nobody watched, because everybody was watching a screen where nothing surprising was happening. Kaiden, who had spent the evening proving that he alone knew the truth, stared at the scoreboard and muttered, "How did they get it right in 1967 and wrong tonight?"

"I'll tell you after you admit the cereal box did my memory," the grandfather said, and held out his hand for a nacho.

activity: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
knowledge_domain: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
fact: In Marxist terms, the bourgeoisie owns the means of production, such as factories and land, while the proletariat owns only its labour and must sell it for wages.
story:
The whiteboard in the library's small study room still bore the ghost of last night's tutoring session, a multiplication grid half erased, and Levi wrote over it in green marker: BENEDICK vs. THE SYSTEM. Jordon, sprawled across two chairs with his copy of Much Ado About Nothing open on his chest, said that wasn't even a Victorian novel, and Levi said fine, then let's do the Dickens Ms. Navarro assigned, the one with the factory.

Benson arrived late, carrying three coffees and an insouciant disregard for the no-drinks sign posted directly above the door. He set one in front of Levi anyway. "You said this was about the passage due Monday," he said. "The one where the mill owner explains himself."

"TheBounderbyspeech," Levi said, and found the page. He had read it three times since Thursday, and each time it had felt different: first like a man bragging, then like a man performing, and finally, on the bus that morning, like something he couldn't name but wanted to. He copied a sentence onto the whiteboard, the one where the owner describes pulling himself up from nothing in the gutters.

"Okay," Jordon said, sitting up. "Ms. Navarro gave us the Marxist sheet. It's in my bag." He fished out a photocopied page, creased into eighths, and read aloud: "In Marxist terms, the bourgeoisie owns the means of production, such as factories and land, while the proletariat owns only its labour and must sell it for wages."

Levi uncapped the marker again. Under the speech he drew two columns. "So he's bourgeoisie," he said, tapping the first. "He owns the mill. The land. The actual machines." In the second column he wrote the workers, and after a moment's thought added: nothing but their labour, which they sell him for wages. It looked thin, written that way, almost mathematical, and it made the whole city in the novel feel suddenly legible, like a map he'd been holding upside down.

"That's it?" Benson said. "We sort them like a seating chart and we're done?"

"No, because here's what I keep getting wrong." Levi tapped the speech again. "He says he grew up with nothing. Gutters. No schooling. So the workers in the book, the ones listening to him, believe he's one of them who made it out. And I believed him too, the first time I read it. But if he owns the factory now, he's not one of them anymore, no matter where he started. Or," and this was the part that had kept him awake, "he is one of them and it doesn't matter, which is worse."

Jordon frowned at the columns. "So is the speech a lie or a biography?"

"Maybe both. That's what the lens does, I think. It doesn't tell you who's lying. It tells you what the lying is for." Levi thought of his father, who had spent twenty years selling his hours to a plant outside town and who, whenever anyone criticized management, defended them with a ferocity Levi had never understood until this week. He did not write that on the board. He said instead, "He's like a charlatan who's also his own best customer. He believes his own story because the story indemnifies him. It makes him innocent of the mill."

"Indemnifies," Benson repeated, grinning. "You've been reading the dictionary again."

"Vocabulary sheet, actually. But listen." Levi crossed out the second column's label and wrote only its labour, then crossed that out too and restored the original, because the first version had been the accurate one and he wanted to be accurate even when accuracy was bleak. "Here's what I can't settle. The lens says the owner benefits from the workers and can't see it. Fine. But my dad sees it. He knows exactly what his hours are worth and who keeps the difference. He still defends the plant. Marx can't explain my dad, or the lens can't, and I don't want to write a paragraph pretending it can."

The room went quiet enough that they could hear the automatic doors opening and closing across the lobby, the soft pneumatic sigh of them, someone returning books. Jordon was rereading the photocopy. Benson drank his coffee and looked at the whiteboard as if it were a painting he hadn't decided about yet.

"Then write that," Jordon said finally. "The part you can't settle. Ms. Navarro said an honest complication beats a tidy thesis."

Levi sat down, pulled a notebook toward him, and wrote two sentences, then a third, then crossed out the third and kept the first two. Outside the study room's glass wall, Ms. Navarro passed with a cart of returns, paused, read the whiteboard through the glass, and gave him a small nod before wheeling on toward the stacks.

"So which is he," Benson asked, tipping his cup toward the columns. "Gutter kid or factory owner?"

Levi looked at the board, the green ink drying under the fluorescent light, and said, "Check the deed."

activity: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
knowledge_domain: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
fact: Beyond the Grand Banks of Newfoundland, the Gulf Stream's continuation toward Europe is called the North Atlantic Current or North Atlantic Drift.
story:
The museum had hired him in June, and the remuneration was barely enough to cover bus fare and the deposit on a shared basement room, but Ethan told himself the job was practice: practice for the tour guide certification his college program required, practice for standing in front of strangers and knowing things. So far he had memorized the gift shop inventory and learned to reset the tornado exhibit when toddlers jammed its fan with crackers. The ocean hall was Ms. Henry's territory, and she had handed it to him on Tuesday with a nod and a single sentence, "The school groups will have questions," which he had taken as a warning.

On Thursday the questions arrived wearing matching blue T-shirts from a school two towns over. Ms. Henry stationed herself near the whale skeleton, half-listening, arms folded, and left him alone with a wall-sized map of the Atlantic, animated arrows crawling slowly east, fat and red off the American coast, splitting into paler threads as they crossed toward Europe.

The trouble was a boy in the second row, skinny, persistent, holding a pencil against the glass. "Okay, so this red part is the Gulf Stream," the boy said. "But it stops. Right there." He tapped the middle of the ocean, where the label ended and the arrows continued eastward without a name. "Then what's that?"

"That's the same current," Ethan said, and heard immediately that it was the wrong shape of answer, the shape of a cover for not knowing.

"It's got a different color," the boy said. "So is it different?"

Behind the group, Cynthia had appeared with Megan, both of them museum-bound by the same summer lull, slushies sweating in their hands. Cynthia was bound elsewhere in September, though. She had spent all of spring insisting she was taking the year off, working, saving, staying home with her mother, and only last week she had let Ethan read the deferral-cancellation email on her phone, saying nothing while he read it. He had congratulated her. He had also, he noticed, felt something contract in his chest, a small unfair resentment he had not managed to dislodge since.

He could have called Ms. Henry over. Instead he crouched at the case beneath the map, where the laminated reference cards lived, and flipped past tides and salinity until he found a diagram keyed to the wall. The fat red arrow off America carried the words Gulf Stream. East of a marked shallows, beyond the Grand Banks of Newfoundland, the continuation toward Europe had its own entries, two of them, alternative names for the same water.

"It's called the North Atlantic Current," Ethan said, standing. "Or the North Atlantic Drift. Same thing, two names. It's the Gulf Stream continuing, past the Grand Banks, toward Europe."

"So why does the map stop calling it that?" the boy asked.

"Honestly? I think the map makers gave up. The water's the same water, it just spreads out and slows down, and somewhere out there somebody drew a line and said, new name past here." Ethan hadn't known that a minute ago, and the boy seemed to register it, to file him in a new category, someone honest about the edges of his own map. The follow-up question, though, came from Megan, who had drifted forward, straw between her teeth.

"Explain the Europe thing, then. My dad says Scotland has palm trees because of this current. That can't be real."

Ethan put his hand flat on the glass, tracing the arrows east, and said that Scotland sat at about the same latitude as Hudson Bay, which froze solid in winter, and that Britain did not, and that the difference was this water moving warmth north and east across the whole ocean. "Lisbon is level with New York," he added, "but nobody's shoveling snow off the Portuguese beaches in April." It was the first fully formed thing he had explained all summer, and something in him sat up.

"Problem solved, then," Cynthia said, but she said it lightly, and her eyes went to the far wall, where a panel about warming oceans listed species whose ranges were shifting north, cod among them, declines described as endemic to the region. "Except look at that. It warms Europe, and it's also the thing changing on them." She tilted her head. "You can't just teach the pretty version."

Ethan had spent a month wanting the pretty version, wanting the clean diagram and the confident answer, and standing there he understood that her instinct was right and also that it complicated everything he'd rehearsed. Every fact he'd memorized could be problematized by the next panel over, and a good explainer had to hold both, the mechanism and the worry, without pretending either away.

Ms. Henry drifted over as the group moved on. She looked at the map, then at Ethan, and said only, "You found the cards. Good." Later, when the hall had emptied and the overhead lights dimmed to their evening amber, Cynthia stood beside him at the wall, slushie long gone.

"So you're doing this for real now," she said. "The job. The program in the fall."

"I'm doing something," Ethan said. "Ask me in September."

She laughed, tapped the glass over the unnamed stretch of ocean between the two labels, and said, "Same water, though."

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: Montana is the one US state where, after a probationary period, an employer generally needs good cause to fire a worker, under its 1987 Wrongful Discharge from Employment Act.
story:
The application said the interview would take fifteen minutes, and Jason had decided to believe it, because believing it was the only thing keeping his hands dry. He'd told his mother he wasn't nervous at all. He'd also told her he'd eaten breakfast, which was likewise untrue, and the two lies had reinforced each other so well that by the time he pushed through the door of the restaurant at 3:52, he felt almost honest.

Behind the counter, in the booth by the window, Benoit and Nick were arguing over a shared order of fries. This was normal. What was not normal was that their argument was about the exact thing Jason had spent the last twenty-four hours reading about, and he had not told them he was reading about it.

"Your cousin's wrong," Nick was saying. "A boss can fire you for anything. Bad mood, ugly shoes, no reason. That's how it works everywhere."

"Not everywhere. Not Montana."

"Oh, here we go."

"Montana," Benoit said, with the patience of someone repeating scripture, "is the one state where, after a probationary period, an employer generally needs good cause to fire a worker. It's called the Wrongful Discharge from Employment Act. 1987."

Jason slid into the booth beside them, and they barely looked up. This was the arrangement: he was allowed to sit with them before things, as long as he understood he was third in line for fries.

"My cousin got fired for being in a bad mood," Jason said. "Michigan. My mom says he deserved it."

"Your mom," said Nick, "has never met your cousin."

That was fair. His mother had met the cousin once, at a funeral, and formed an opinion so durable it had survived no further contact. Jason sometimes suspected his own opinions worked the same way, assembled from one conversation and then defended like territory.

"Look it up," Benoit said. "I'm right. Everywhere except Montana, after probation or whatever, they can basically just fire you. In Montana they need good cause."

"Fine," Nick said, and took out his phone, which was the closest Nick ever came to conceding anything.

The clock above the drink station said 3:56. The manager, Mr. Visser, was at the register, counting something, unhurried in a way that suggested time worked differently on his side of the counter. Jason had four minutes, and he spent one of them verbalize-adjacent: rehearsing, under his breath, the sentence "I'm available weekends and most weeknights," which he then realized was not a sentence he could truthfully say and would have to amend at the counter, live.

"You know the probation period here is thirty days," Benoit said, apropos of nothing Jason had said aloud, which was unsettling. "My brother worked here. Thirty days, then they either keep you or they don't, and after that it takes more to get rid of you. Not Montana-level, but still."

"It's not a competition," Nick said.

"Everything is a competition."

The phone had confirmed Montana. Nick read the number out, 1987, and the name again, Wrongful Discharge from Employment Act, in the flat tone of a man reading his own defeat into the record. Jason filed this away. Somewhere in his head, two things were being laid against each other: the fact that a job could end at any moment for no reason, and the fact that in one state it mostly couldn't. Both felt true. Neither seemed to have much to do with him standing up in eight seconds and asking a man for recompense in the form of minimum wage.

"Jason." Mr. Visser had come around the counter without Jason noticing, a clipboard under his arm. "You're the four o'clock."

"I'm the four o'clock," Jason agreed, standing too fast and banging his knee on the table leg in a way that felt tectonic, at least to him, though the table did not move.

Mr. Visser led him to the second booth, the one without the friends in it, and set down the clipboard. The questions were the questions. Availability, transportation, whether he could work the fry station during a rush. Jason answered the last one honestly, which was to say no, but he said it in a voice that suggested no was a temporary condition, like weather.

Then Mr. Visser said the thing Jason had not prepared for. "I'll be straight with you. Last kid I hired I let go in three weeks. Didn't cut it. I don't love doing that, but that's the job." He turned a page. "You still want it?"

Jason thought about his cousin in Michigan, fired for a mood. He thought about Montana, where firing apparently required something better than a mood, after probation, generally, 1987, and he thought about how none of that would be true here on Saturday when he was burning the nuggets. He could hold both ideas. The job was precarious. The job was also money, and Saturdays, and something to say when relatives asked what he was doing these days.

"Yes," he said. "I want it."

Mr. Visser slid the pen across the table. Behind them, Nick had begun arguing that the website was outdated, and Benoit was saying, "Fine, call your cousin," and reaching for the phone, dialing, while the fry basket hissed and the clock over the drinks said 4:03.

"Sign there," said Mr. Visser, "and there," and Jason, without reading paragraph four, did.

activity: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
knowledge_domain: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
fact: TinEye, a reverse image search engine launched in 2008, can sort results with the oldest first, helping find when an image first appeared online.
story:
Eloic's kitchen smelled like burnt popcorn and energy drink, and his phone lay face-up on the counter, playing the same twelve seconds on a loop. It showed a bridge buckling, a kind of long metal shriek, and a caption in red: THIS IS HAPPENING RIGHT NOW. He'd already sent it to the group chat before Brayden had his shoes off.

"Fourteen shares in ten minutes," Eloic said. "Leanne's uncle is a civil engineer and she's asking him if bridges do that."

Brayden leaned over the counter. Something about the light in the video bothered him, a flatness he couldn't name, and he said so. Eloic told him he sounded like a guy who didn't want anyone to have fun, which was fair, since last month Brayden had forwarded a shark on a highway during a flood and spent two days being quietly wrong about it. A shark, on a highway, that he had personally vouched for. His mother still brought it up at dinner.

"That's different," Brayden said. "That was a flood. Floods make anything believable."

"So bridges make nothing believable?"

"I didn't say that." But he was already pulling out his own phone, not to argue, exactly. It was more that the video had a feeling of having happened before, the way certain afternoons presage rain without a cloud in sight, and he wanted to catch it out.

Leanne arrived with her laptop under her arm because her phone screen was cracked and, she claimed, the crack made everything look like a war zone anyway, so she couldn't judge video footage on principle. She set the laptop on the counter next to the popcorn bowl. "My uncle says bridges can do that if the cables snap," she reported. "He also says, and I quote, where and when, because context is everything. He's very fun at parties."

"Context," Eloic said, "is that it's happening right now. It says so."

"The caption says so," Brayden said.

Eloic made a gesture that took in the whole kitchen, the popcorn, the afternoon, as evidence that Brayden was getting heavy about a video. "You want to be the guy who fact-checks a disaster? That's a whole personality."

But Leanne, who was already typing, said, "You can search an image backwards. You take a screenshot and instead of searching words you search the picture. It finds where else it's been." She turned the laptop so Brayden could see. "There's one called TinEye. It's been around since 2008, which is somehow older than us feeling right now." She dropped the screenshot in and the results loaded, a long column of pages containing the same buckling bridge.

Brayden took over the trackpad. There was a sort option at the top of the results, and he changed it to oldest first, and the column reshuffled itself, and the top result was dated years ago. Not hours. Not today. Years. A news site, a headline about an inspection failure, a date that belonged to a version of the world where he'd been maybe thirteen and hadn't yet forwarded a shark anywhere.

Nobody said anything for a second. The microwave hummed behind them, pointless now, its work done.

"It was real, though," Eloic said finally, and this was the part Brayden kept turning over later, because Eloic wasn't entirely wrong. "The bridge did that. It happened. So what did I do wrong?"

"It happened," Brayden agreed. "Just not now, and not to the people you just scared." He scrolled the older results. Different captions on the same footage over the years, each one urgent, each one certain. The video was like a coin that had been spent over and over in different vending machines. He put that out loud, more or less, and Leanne said the metaphor was doing a lot of work, but she said it approvingly.

Eloic sat with his phone in his hand, thumb over the group chat. "So do I post a correction? 'Hey everyone, the bridge is fine, it was fine years ago, please continue your day of hedonism in peace.'" He was joking, but only by about forty percent. He had forwarded it first, and being first with something wrong was its own particular tax, one Brayden had paid at his own dinner table.

"That or nothing," Leanne said. "A correction on its own just shows the video again."

Brayden thought about the gap between the two of them: Eloic wanted the video to be true because sharing it had felt like participating in the world, and Brayden wanted it false because being wrong had once cost him something small but memorable. Neither of those was actually about the bridge. He said none of this, because saying it would have made him the guy with a whole personality, and instead he asked Eloic whether his uncle, the civil engineer, had said anything about which bridge it was, whether that detail was germane to the original story or just to the new one.

They found the original article together, Leanne reading over his shoulder, and there was a name of a place none of them had heard of and a quote from an official about maintenance budgets. There was no way to know, from the article alone, whether the re-posting was a lie or just carelessness, someone grabbing a dramatic clip because it performed well, and Brayden noticed that he couldn't make himself care about the difference as much as he felt he should. The footage was old. That part was solid. The rest of it, motive and meaning, stayed soft.

Eloic typed something into the group chat, deleted it, typed again, and finally sent a single message: not a correction, just a link to the old article with no comment. Then he closed the app with a decisive tap, as if the tap were the whole apology.

Leanne was already clicking through TinEye's other tabs, and she said, idly, that you could probably do this with anything, any photo, anyone's picture, find out where it had been before it got to you. She looked up at both of them. "That's a little terrifying, right?"

Brayden screenshotted the oldest result and saved it to his phone, next to the shark.

activity: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
knowledge_domain: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
fact: Ignoring air resistance, the horizontal distance a projectile travels equals its constant horizontal velocity multiplied by its time in the air.
story:
Joseph had failed the last physics test by four points, and Mr. Barrett had told him that if he wanted to retake it, he needed to show up understanding projectiles, not just memorizing formulas. So on a Saturday in October he sat on an overturned milk crate in Mr. Barrett's garage with his textbook on his knees and Zayne crouched beside the workbench, spinning a lug nut on the concrete for no reason.

"You're doing it wrong," Zayne said, not looking up. "You keep plugging numbers into that one big equation. Dhruv does the split thing."

"The split thing isn't wrong," Joseph said. "It's just not what I do yet."

Mr. Barrett was at his lathe in the corner, turning a length of brass rod into something for a lamp he was rebuilding. When he wasn't teaching at the high school he was out here most weekends, and he had let Joseph know, without ever saying it in a speech, that the garage was open to a boy who brought his own book. The lathe made a sound like steady rain.

Zayne flicked the lug nut across the floor and it clipped the leg of Joseph's crate. "Throw something. You've got a whole garage."

Joseph picked up a tennis ball from a bucket of dog toys by the door. He tossed it straight up, caught it. The vertical problem was the one he could do: up and down was just free fall, gravity chewing the velocity at the top until the ball hung there for half a breath and came back down. Time in the air, that he could find.

"Okay," he said. "Watch." He rolled the ball sideways along the floor, smooth and low, so it crossed the garage at a steady rate and knocked a soft note off the base of the trash can. "That's the sideways one. It doesn't slow down. It just goes."

"Nothing slows it down," Zayne said. "Floor's smooth."

"Ignore friction, whatever. That's the whole point." He was half talking to the book now. He stood, walked the ball's path heel to toe, and counted his strides. Eleven steps, each about a meter. He had rolled it and counted nothing else, no stopwatch, and that bothered him; the problem in front of him, number twenty-three, had a stone leaving a cliff at twelve meters per second sideways and falling from a height of twenty meters, and it wanted the landing distance.

"Twenty meters down," he said. "Free fall from rest sideways, so vertical's just the drop. Two seconds." He had done that arithmetic twice already; it hadn't changed. And then he sat very still on the crate, because the two seconds were the same two seconds. The stone was in the air for two seconds whether you watched it fall or watched it slide. And the sideways speed never changed, twelve the whole way, no gravity pulling it left or right, gravity only worked up and down.

"So twelve for two seconds," he said. "That's twenty-four. Twenty-four meters from the cliff." He wrote it and looked at the number as if someone else had produced it. One more multiplication after the flight time and the landing point just appeared, the way the trash can had appeared in the path of the ball.

Dhruv arrived then, bicycle helmet still buckled, having ridden the four blocks because his mother had the car. He read the problem off Joseph's page in about six seconds. "Twenty-four," he said. "Yeah. You find the time first, then multiply."

"That's what I got," Joseph said, and heard how defensive it came out, so he said it again plainly. "That's what I got. Sideways distance is the sideways speed, which never changes, times the time in the air. That's all it is."

Zayne had stopped spinning the lug nut. "So the throw and the fall are the same fall."

"They're two problems that share a clock," Joseph said. It was the first thing in three weeks that had come out of him sounding like his own thinking and not like a page he'd copied. He had been treating physics as a set of unrelated formulas to be matched to problems, the way Mr. Barrett treated each repair as its own job, but the garage was teaching him something different, a kind of mutualism between the two halves of one throw: the vertical part does you a favor by giving up the time, and the horizontal part spends that time traveling, neither one useful alone.

Mr. Barrett shut off the lathe and looked at the brass rod, which had gone from a bar to something thin and ductile under his tool, curled slightly where the blade had pressed it. He weighed it in his hand without turning around. "Insurance ran out on that retake," he said. "It's Tuesday or nothing. You indemnify yourself by knowing it cold."

"I think I know it," Joseph said.

"Then prove it with something you can't look up." He set the brass down and nodded at the bucket by the door. "Toss one off the stepladder."

Joseph carried the ball to the top of the folded ladder, climbed until his head was near the ceiling, and stood there working it out before he threw it: the height gave him the time, the time would give the distance, and the sideways push of his hand would be the whole horizontal story, unchanged all the way down. He could even fix where it landed by choosing how hard to throw. He tossed it, not straight down and not straight out, and the ball struck the concrete between the crate and the trash can, bounced twice, and rolled to rest against Dhruv's shoe.

"Nine meters a second," Dhruv read off his phone timer. "Roughly."

Joseph climbed down and chalked the spot where it had hit.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: The Suzuki method, developed by Japanese violinist Shinichi Suzuki, teaches children to play by ear before reading music, the way they learn to speak before reading.
story:
The community center rented its rooms by the hour, and on Thursday evenings the room with the piano and the folding chairs belonged to whoever showed up with an instrument. Madeline arrived at six with her rented violin, a shoulder rest that pinched, and a music stand she still could not fold correctly. She had been playing for five months. She could read the notes. She could not, apparently, make them sound like anything.

The problem was simple and infuriating: she read music well enough that her eyes led and her ears followed. Mr. Novák, who ran the Thursday sessions as a favor to the center, had noticed it by the third week. "You stop when the page surprises you," he said. "The page should not be able to surprise you that much."

Across the room, a boy of about eight was playing "Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star" from memory, then playing it starting on a different note, then playing it backward, giggling when he lost the thread. Madeline had heard him before and had assumed he was showing off. Tonight she stopped packing up to listen. He could not read a single note on the staff. When Mr. Novák held up a sheet of the same tune, the boy looked at it the way Madeline looked at assembly instructions for furniture she had already built wrong.

"How does he do that?" she asked.

Matias, who played cello in the corner and liked to narrate, shrugged. "He's Suzuki. My little cousin does it too. The Suzuki method, from that Japanese teacher, Shinichi Suzuki. It teaches kids to play by ear before they read music. Like learning to speak before you learn to read."

Madeline turned this over while the boy launched into a scale she recognized but could not have produced without paper. She had spent five months decoding. He had spent, apparently, two years speaking. It struck her as unjust, and then as interesting, and she was honest enough with herself to admit she could not decide which it truly was.

The next Thursday she brought her folder of etudes and did not open it. Instead she asked the boy, whose name was Danny, to play the first phrase of one of her pieces, a slow waltz from a book two levels above hers. He played it twice. She listened, then picked up her violin and copied him, haltingly, missing the F sharp, finding it, missing it again.

"You're guessing," Danny said, not unkindly.

"I'm listening badly," she said. "There's a difference."

Tiffany, who had come from the pottery studio down the hall to wait for her ride, expostulated from the doorway that this was a waste of a good lesson, that Madeline had a perfectly decent ear-training app on her phone, and that anyone could learn intervals in six weeks if they practiced on the bus. Madeline said maybe. She had the app. The app had not changed anything, and she suspected it was because the app treated listening as a quiz rather than as a way of getting music into her hands.

She kept at it for a month. She would bring a piece home, play the recording while she washed dishes, then try to pull it out of the violin without the page. Some nights it worked a phrase at a time. Some nights she gave up and read the notes, and noticed, with a small odd satisfaction, that reading felt different now, more like a record of something she might have said than a set of orders. She did not think one way was better. Reading let her play things too long to memorize. Playing by ear let the waltz sound, on one memorable Tuesday, like it belonged to her. She suspected the two were not opposites so much as two doors into the same room, though she could not have proved it, and she stopped trying to.

Mr. Novák, who had opinions about almost everything, including Matias's habit of tuning his cello during other people's attempts, and the center's munificent but perpetually detuned piano, and the idiosyncrasy of Thursday scheduling that put the drum circle next door, said almost nothing about any of this. At the end of the month he put a piece on her stand, unplayed, and said, "Read it once, then put the page down."

She read it once. She put the page face-down on the chair. She raised the violin, and in the silence before the first note she could hear Danny, next door or somewhere, whistling his backward "Twinkle" tune.

She began.

activity: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
knowledge_domain: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
fact: Le Chatelier's principle states that when a system at equilibrium is disturbed, the equilibrium shifts in the direction that partly counteracts the change.
story:
The clock above the whiteboard gave them twenty minutes, and Mr. Tan had already said twice that the sealed tubes had to be back in the rack before the bell. Annabelle lined up her three tubes on the bench: one pale pink, one violet, one the deep blue of a cold lake. Her partner, Mataya, was voluble even in whispers, narrating everything she touched, and Annabelle had learned over two years of lab partnerships to let that noise wash past her without desensitizing her entirely, because sometimes buried in it was something worth keeping.

"Write your prediction first," Mr. Tan said from the front. "Before the water bath. If you look and then predict, it doesn't count." He said it without gravitas, almost wearily, the way a man says something he has said to eleven classes already, but Annabelle wrote it at the top of her page anyway, underlined it, and then sat there with her pen not moving.

The problem was that she had two ideas in her head and they disagreed. In chemistry, equilibrium meant the forward and reverse reactions happening at the same rate, so the amounts of everything stayed steady, like a standstill that was secretly busy. But heat, she thought, speeds things up, so shouldn't heating just make everything faster and leave the standstill standing? Then there was what Leila had said at lunch, leaning across the table with her sandwich held aloft: "It's Le Chatelier's principle, obviously. When you disturb a system at equilibrium, it shifts in the direction that partly counteracts the change." Leila had said it the way she said everything, as though the universe were a rumor she had been first to hear.

Annabelle did not trust Leila's confidence, which was vast and occasionally wrong. But she did trust the sentence itself, because she'd copied it from the textbook herself. What she could not see was which direction "counteracts" meant here. The tube in her hand was sealed, the liquid sealed in with its purple cloudiness, and somewhere in it two forms of the same dissolved stuff sat balanced. If she added heat, which way would it lean?

"Seven minutes for predictions," said Mr. Tan.

"Write pink," Mataya whispered. "Heat makes things pink. Like, warm colors for warm water."

"That's not a reason, that's a vibe."

"It's a heuristic." Mataya said the word carefully, pleased with it.

Annabelle drew two arrows on her page, one pointing each way, and stared at them. Adding heat was a change. If the equilibrium were going to counteract a change, it would have to lean toward whatever used the heat up, took it in, rather than whatever pushed it back out. That much followed from Leila's sentence, the same way a shadow follows a body. So the question became: which direction in this tube took heat in? She didn't know. She looked at the tube and it told her nothing; it was a sealed system, sealed precisely so that nothing could escape and complicate things, just the balanced mixture and whatever she did to its temperature.

She thought about her mother's recipe for proofing bread, how the dough sat quietly at room temperature, apparently finished, and how moving it somewhere warm changed what it was. Two worlds, the kitchen and the lab, and she was trying to make them hold hands. The dough didn't fight the warmth; it leaned into it, used it. Maybe the reaction did the same, tilting toward the side that swallowed the change she'd made, and only partly, because the principle said partly, not fully, which meant the tilt was a compromise, not a cure.

"Pink going blue or blue going pink?" Mataya demanded. "Four minutes."

"Blue," Annabelle said. "If heat is the disturbance, the shift goes toward the direction that uses heat up, and I think that's the blue side. But I'm not sure which side that is. That's the part I can't get from the sentence alone." She wrote her prediction in full, including the uncertainty, and her handwriting got smaller as the time did.

They lowered the tubes into the water bath with the tongs, and Mr. Tan counted the seconds out loud because the thermometers were shared. The violet tube went in violet. It came out, thirty seconds later, undeniably pinker, the color draining from it like dusk running out of sky, and Mataya made a small wounded sound.

"Wrong," Mataya said. "I said pink, I said pink first."

"You said pink for a bad reason. Being right by accident is worse." But Annabelle was barely arguing; she was holding the warm tube up to the window, watching the last of the blue fade. Her prediction had been wrong too, in its specifics, though the shape of her thinking, disturb it and it shifts partway to counteract, was still standing under her. What she'd gotten wrong was the map of this particular tube, which side was which, and that, she saw now, was something no principle could hand you. You had to run the bath.

The second tube, the one she'd kept out of the bath as a control, sat on the bench still violet, indifferent, balanced. She put them side by side and copied both into her notebook, drawing the colors as best she could with the two pens she had.

"Time," called Mr. Tan.

Annabelle capped her pen. "Tomorrow I'm asking Leila which side is which before I predict anything," she said. "Not after."

Mataya was already sliding the tubes back into the rack, blue end first, the way the diagram on the wall showed, and the pink one caught the light one last time before it clicked into its slot.

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
knowledge_domain: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
fact: Properly tempered chocolate shrinks slightly as it sets, which helps it release cleanly from a mould.
story:
The restaurant kitchen smelled of burnt sugar and dish soap, and Cameron had been peeling failed chocolates out of silicone moulds for twenty minutes. Each one came out dull, streaked grey where it should have been glossy, and half of them tore at the rim. He stacked the casualties on a sheet pan while the lunch rush thundered on the other side of the swing doors, waiters calling tickets, the fryer hissing like something with a grievance.

"They look like fossils," Kylie said, leaning over his shoulder. She worked the salad station on Saturdays, and she had appointed herself the kitchen's unofficial critic, a position she held without anyone's permission. "Like something we dug up."

Cameron set another ruined shell on the pan. He had begged Ms. Morningstar for the pastry apprenticeship, had promised his mother he would stop treating every job like a temporary inconvenience, and for three weekends the chocolate had defeated him. He melted it, he cooled it, he stirred it on the marble slab the way the old pastry text described, and still the shells came out matte and stuck.

Ms. Morningstar swept through on her way to the walk-in, paused, and tapped one mould with her knuckle. "What did you do after you seeded it?"

"I poured it," Cameron said. "Right away. The batch was thin and shiny, so I figured it was ready."

She looked at him for a moment longer than was comfortable, the way she did when she wanted him to arrive somewhere on his own. Then the ticket printer shrieked and she was gone, and Cameron was left holding a mould with two halves fused inside it like something that had decided to stay.

Fatoumata came in at four for the dinner prep, tying her apron, and found him still at it. She was the only other student from his school who worked weekends, and they had an arrangement: he explained her chemistry homework, she told him when he was being ridiculous. "You're going to litigate that mould all night," she said. "It's chocolate, not a defendant."

"It's personal at this point."

She picked up the pastry text he'd propped against the vinegar bottles, its spine cracked, a paperback his mother had bought used. She turned pages with one finger. "Here. This bit."

Cameron read the passage twice. Properly tempered chocolate shrinks slightly as it sets, which helps it release cleanly from a mould. He turned the mould over in his hands and pressed his thumb against the back of one cavity. The stuck shells sat flush against the silicone, tight as a cork in a bottle, as if they had never moved at all. If the chocolate had shrunk, even a little, there would have been a gap. A slack. Something to work with.

"Tempered chocolate shrinks a little while it sets," he said slowly. "That's what pulls it away from the mould." He looked up. "Mine never shrank. It just sat there and solidified exactly where I poured it. So it was never in temper at all. The shine was fake. It was just hot."

"So what went wrong before the pour?"

He thought about the marble slab, the way the book said to cool the chocolate to a working temperature, testing a dab on his lip like a mother with a bottle, and how he had skipped that because the bowl looked right. He had trusted appearance over process, the way he trusted a lot of things, and it occurred to him that this was a habit with a history. He didn't say that part out loud. Fatoumata was already dragging the tempered couverture and a clean bench scraper toward the slab.

"You're going to do it right now," she said. "Before service. I'll time you."

He melted the chocolate gently, poured two thirds of it onto the marble, and worked it with the scraper in long folds, watching it thicken and lose its shine, then lose a little more, until the dab on his lip felt faintly cool. When he added the reserved warm chocolate back and stirred, the batch flowed like something with structure in it, and he poured it into the mould with more care than he had ever given anything, tapping out the bubbles, sliding it into the cooler.

Kylie wandered by during her break and organized a plebiscite among the dishwashers on whether Cameron's chocolates would stick again, ballots cast on paper towels, unanimous in their pessimism. "You have a congenital inability to wait for things," she announced, "so this is a character test."

Twelve minutes later he flexed the mould over the sheet pan, one quick snap of the wrist, and the shells dropped out in a neat row, glossy as piano keys, each one whole. Fatoumata picked one up and broke it against the counter's edge and it snapped clean, audibly, like a small door closing. Cameron held the mould up to the light, looking at the empty cavities, the faint even gap where the chocolate had drawn away from the sides, and he was already planning the next batch, because one success was only evidence, not proof, and he wanted to know if he could do it twice.

"Ten minutes till you're on salads," Fatoumata said, and handed him the broken half she was saving for him.

activity: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
knowledge_domain: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
fact: In Kahlo's The Broken Column (1944), her spine is painted as a cracked Ionic column visible through an opening in her body.
story:
Henry spread the printout on the picnic table and weighted its corners with rocks, because the August wind in Mr. Sinclair's backyard had opinions of its own. The painting was small on the page, a woman standing in a cracked landscape, and Henry had been staring at it for two days without producing a single sentence his art history teacher would accept. The assignment demanded formal analysis, colour, composition, symbolism, and Henry had written only a question in the margin of his notebook: why is there a Greek column inside her?

Alena came through the gap in the fence with two glasses of lemonade, one of which she set at Henry's elbow without comment. She had a way of doing that, meeting a need before it was announced, and he had grown so inured to it that he only noticed when she didn't. Adriano followed her, dropped onto the bench, and pulled the page toward himself with the confidence of someone who had taken exactly one semester of art appreciation.
