"She's sad," Adriano said. "That's the symbolism. Sad woman, sad painting."

"That's not analysis, that's a greeting card." Alena leaned over the print, squinting. "Look at the colour, though. Everything's beige and brown and cracked, like the ground and the sky are made of the same dead skin. Except the sheet she's holding, and that thing in the middle."

That thing was what had stopped Henry. It ran vertically through the woman's torso, white and segmented, broken across the middle, and it showed through a tear in her skin as if her body were a curtain pulled aside. Around it, small nails punctured her face and limbs and the sheet below. He had assumed the nails were the point, the obvious part, but the column kept refusing to be decoration.

"It's architecture," Henry said slowly. "A column. From a building." He turned to his notebook and sketched it quickly, the fluted shaft, the break. "Greek, maybe. Ionic, the kind with the scrolls on top, you can just see them at her chest." He looked up. "So the painting puts a building inside a person. Her spine is the cracked column, and the opening in her body is what lets us see it."

Adriano frowned at the sketch. "So she's a house that's falling down."

"That's a syllogism, not a reading," Alena said, though she said it gently, and when Adriano's ears went red she added, "but it's not wrong either. Henry, use it. Formal analysis is just this, describing what your eye does and then asking why."

The screen door banged and Mr. Sinclair crossed his own grass with a plate of sliced peaches, another unneeded kindness offered as though it were nothing. He set the plate down, glanced at the printout, and hummed. "The Broken Column. My wife kept a poster of it in her studio for thirty years." He did not lecture, which Henry appreciated; he only ate a peach slice and said, "She used to say the hardest thing about that painting is that the column doesn't scream. It just stands there, broken, holding whatever it still holds."

Henry wrote that down before he could decide whether it was cheating. Then he wrote other things, fast, while the wind worried the rocks. That the composition divides the body the way the background divides earth from sky, so figure and landscape share one grammar of fracture. That the palette is spartan, almost no colour except the red of the opened body and the blue of that small strip of sheet, so those two patches do the work of everything she cannot say with a face full of nails. That the symbolism is not the nails, which anyone can feel, but the column, which you have to know something to see: an ancient, rational, load-bearing thing, cracked but upright, inside a woman standing in a desert with tears on her cheeks and her feet planted anyway.

He was less sure about the rest. Whether the column meant endurance or collapse or both at once, whether a painting this personal could still be read formally without flattening it, whether his paragraph on theIonic capital, its scrolls like small closed fists, was insight or decoration. He underlined a sentence he liked and then drew a question mark beside the underline, and let both stand.

Alena refilled his lemonade without being asked. Adriano pulled the sketch toward himself again and began copying the column onto the back of Henry's notebook, badly, adding a face. Mr. Sinclair collected the peach plate, paused at the fence, and said, "She painted it in the year I was born, you know." Then he was through the gate, and the wind flipped one corner of the printout free of its rock, and Henry reached out and held the painting flat with the flat of his hand.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: A violin's four strings are tuned in perfect fifths to G, D, A and E, from lowest to highest.
story:
Claire had wanted the violin for exactly one reason: it fit in a locker. The cello would have meant a second bus seat and a negotiation with her mother about the trunk of the car, but the violin slid into its case like a secret, and she had carried it into Ms. Becker's studio on the first Tuesday of September with the confidence of someone who had never heard herself play.

"You're holding it like a baguette," said Amos, who had been taking lessons here for three years and seemed to consider the studio his personal kingdom. He was sprawled on the bench by the window, waiting for his own lesson, eating something that crumbled onto the sheet music Ms. Becker kept on the radiator.

"I'm holding it with dignity," Claire said. She had, in fact, watched eleven tutorial videos that morning, and each one had ended with the instructor saying the word "relax" in a tone that made relaxing impossible.

Ms. Becker tuned the instrument for her that first week, walking her fingers across the strings while Claire memorized the geography by feel. It was the fourth lesson before the trouble started, because Ms. Becker, in a moment of optimism, handed her the tuning fork and said, "You try."

Claire plucked the fattest string and turned the peg. The note climbed, wavered, climbed. Behind her, Amos winced like a man being personally injured.

"That's your G," he said. "You're torturing your G."

"It's a string, not a hostage."

"Lowest string, G," he said, and then, because he could never leave a good thing alone, he chanted it like a dumb rhyme from middle school. "G, D, A, E. All in perfect fifths, going up. Lowest to highest. G-D-A-E."

"Is that supposed to help?"

"It's the whole violin. That's the entire secret. My brain wouldn't keep it until I made it into a song." He sang it then, horribly, to the tune of the school's fight song, and Ms. Becker laughed into her coffee, and Claire laughed too, and then she wrote the four letters on the inside of her left wrist in gel pen before she even left the studio.

The problem, she discovered over the following week, was that she kept half remembering it. In her bedroom on Thursday she confidently tuned her lowest string to D, and the whole instrument sounded like a door complaining. She called Amos, who answered with his mouth full. "G first," he said. "G, then D, then A, then E. Fifths all the way up. Write it on your hand again, or get it tattooed, I don't care."

The odd thing was how much the ordering came to matter to her beyond the tuning itself. Her mother, who had opinions about everything, had opinions about this too: that music lessons were an extrinsic decoration on a college application, that what mattered was the transcript, the annuity of good grades compounding quietly year after year. "Nobody ever got a scholarship for the violin," her mother said at dinner, in the voice she used for facts.

"Amos did," Claire said. It wasn't quite true; Amos had gotten a scholarship for the violin plus his grades plus an essay about his grandfather, but the correction felt extrinsic to the argument, so she left it out. Her mother looked at her for a long moment, then served herself more rice, which in their household was a concession.

What Claire could not explain, even to herself, was that she practiced now not for the application and not against her mother but because of the order of the thing. Four strings, each one a perfect fifth above the last, G climbing to D climbing to A climbing to E, a ladder with evenly spaced rungs that her fingers were slowly learning to find in the dark. When she got it right, the instrument sounded like it had been designed by someone with a tidy mind, and when she got it wrong, it sounded like the truth: that she was seventeen and guessing.

At the next lesson she tuned it herself, all four strings, no fork, and Ms. Becker made her do it twice more just to watch. Amos applauded with two pencils, dangerously, from the bench.

"Encore," he said. "Do it blindfolded."

"Next month," Claire said. She lifted the bow, set it on the A string, which she now knew was the third one up, and drew out a note that cracked in the middle like an egg.

"Beautiful," Amos said. "Truly. My ears are suturing themselves back together as we speak."

"Get out," said Ms. Becker, but she was smiling, and she was already writing something in the margin of Claire's book, a piece for next week, one with an E string passage marked in red.

activity: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
knowledge_domain: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
fact: Circumlocution, describing a word you cannot remember instead of stopping, is a recognized communication strategy that keeps a second-language speaker talking.
story:
The kitchen timer on Ludovic's counter was set to five minutes, and Sierra had already false-started twice. The assignment from Ms. Wilson's class was simple to state and monstrous to do: take a position on the city's new carbon tax and defend it for five minutes, entirely in French, no notes, no English lifeline. Ludovic's mother had cleared out the dinner dishes and left them to it, and Johnathan sat at the table with the timer like a bailiff waiting to read a verdict.

"Encore," Ludovic said, which meant again, and Sierra understood it as a small acquittal of the first two attempts, a pardon granted on the condition she not repeat the crime.

She began well. The tax on fuel, she argued, was the least dishonest way to pay for what burning fuel costs everyone. Then she reached for the word and it was gone. Not the idea, the word, the plain French word for tax that she had known since September. Johnathan's pencil hovered over the score sheet. She felt the incipient panic, the cold spreading through her grammar, and then she did something she had not planned. She kept going. It is, she said, a sum of money that the government asks from people when they buy petrol, a payment that follows the smoke. Her French was bent and slow around the phrase, but it moved forward.

Ludovic held up a hand, stopped the timer at two minutes, and grinned. "You just did it. What you did is called circumlocution," he said. "Describing the word instead of stopping. Coaches teach it. You did it on your own."

Sierra sat back. She had spent months believing fluency meant never failing to find a word, and here was a door she hadn't known existed: you could forget and still speak. But the cost showed itself immediately. The phrase had taken her eleven seconds, Johnathan told her, reading off the sheet, and in a real debate the other side would use those seconds to cut in. Precision was faster. Talking around a word was survivable but ugly, and she could already imagine opponents who would denigrate an accented, roundabout speaker rather than answer her argument, treating the limp in her language as a limp in her reasoning.

They ran it again. She forgot the word for tax on purpose this time, to practice, and tried a shorter detour, a sum that the state takes at the pump. Six seconds. Then four. Johnathan kept time and shouted the count like a swimming coach, and somewhere in the fourth run she forgot the word for pollution too and described it as what the cars leave in the sky that the lungs pay for, and Ludovic laughed and said that was better than the real word, and she hated how pleased she was, because it wasn't better, it was a substitute, and a substitute is what you settle for.

On the seventh run she went the full five minutes. Her argument had teeth, she thought: she conceded the tax fell harder on people who had to drive far for work, then argued the revenue could rebate them first, then said the alternative was pretending the cost did not exist, which was its own tax, just collected by children not yet born. Ludovic clapped once, the way you clap at a funeral in some countries, quietly and with obligation. Johnathan read the sheet: strong position, good concessions, fluent enough. Ms. Wilson would be satisfied.

Afterward they stood in the driveway eating the last of a bag of chips while Ludovic's mother's sprinklers ticked across the darkening lawn. Sierra felt the strange double weight of it: she had gained a way to keep speaking through her own gaps, and she had also confirmed, in front of witnesses, how large the gaps were. Five minutes of French had never felt so long or so short.

It was Johnathan, in English, easy English, their shared birthright, who asked her what she thought the strongest counterargument would be, the one she'd fear most in the real debate. She opened her mouth and reached for the word for tax, the English word, the word she had known before she knew anything else, and it was not there. She stood in the driveway with chips in her hand, hearing herself say, "It's, you know, what the government takes when you buy something," and Ludovic said, softly, "Trop de français," and the sprinklers kept ticking in the dark.

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: Skimming means reading quickly for the general idea, while scanning means searching a text for one specific detail such as a name or number.
story:
The newspaper cost one euro at the kiosk outside the Lisbon metro station, and Logan's father had bought it every morning since they arrived, though he read only the sports pages and asked Logan to attempt the rest. This was the arrangement: Logan had signed up for Portuguese in the fall, his father had declared a family trip to Portugal "an investment," and now, on the sixth morning, Logan sat at a café table with a short article about a riverside festival, a dictionary app, and a deadline. His father had arranged, through a colleague, for him to meet the colleague's niece, Justine, who was studying journalism in Porto and had agreed to hear him summarize an article aloud that afternoon.

The article was eight sentences long. Logan began at the first word and worked toward the last, hunting each unfamiliar term in the app, and after twenty minutes he had decoded three sentences and lost the thread of what the festival was actually for. He caught himself ruminating on whether he was the kind of person who could learn a language at all, which he recognized as a way of not doing the work. His father, reading the sports page, said something about the home team's goalkeeper that Logan chose not to translate.

A message arrived from Marshall, back home, to whom Logan had been sending daily complaints. He opened it at the table. "You still doing the article thing? My mom says when I study it's like watching a dog try to open a door with its face. Also my phone broke so this is from my brother's number, don't judge the spelling." Logan typed back that the article was winning, that he had looked up the word for "orchestra" twice because he'd forgotten it twice, and that he was supposed to summarize it aloud in four hours to a stranger. Marshall replied with a single thumbs-up, which from Marshall was practically a sonnet.

Justine arrived early, at the café nearest the riverside steps, and ordered a coffee with the ease of someone who had never once feared a menu. She was friendly in the way of people who have agreed to do a favor and intend to enjoy it anyway. She asked, in English, whether he had prepared. He admitted he had prepared a list of forty vocabulary words and no summary.

She slid the newspaper across the table and pointed at the article. "What day does the festival start?"

Logan began again at the first sentence, but Justine stopped him with a flat hand, the gesture of a crossing guard. "You don't need the whole thing for that. You need one detail. That's called scanning, searching the text for something specific, a name or a number. Skimming means reading quickly for the general idea. Two different jobs. You're doing neither. You're doing word by word, which is a third job, and it's the slowest one on earth."

Logan felt this land somewhere between insult and revelation. He covered the article with his hands, then slid them away and let his eyes move fast over the lines, refusing to stop at anything he didn't know, the way you let your gaze pass over a crowd looking for one particular coat. The dates in Portuguese were not hard; they sat in the third sentence like coins on a pavement. He found them. Then, feeling bolder, he skimmed the whole piece once for the shape of it, and a surprising amount arrived: boats, a saint, a mayor, music at night. Not perfect. But a festival, with a shape.

He summarized it aloud, slowly, and Justine listened with her chin propped on her fist. When he finished she said, "You said the boats go out to honor the mayor." Logan checked. The boats honored the saint; the mayor only gave a speech. They laughed about the difference, Logan mostly at himself, and Justine observed that knowing which words mattered was not grammar but something she called pragmatics, the study of what language is actually doing to people, and that it was, in her opinion, the only part worth teaching. Logan asked whether the boat detail was germane to his summary or just decoration. She shrugged. "You decide. You're the one summarizing."

Walking back along the river, Logan considered what he now believed, which was two things at once: that reading fast and reading well were not enemies, and that they were not the same thing either. What he still couldn't say was where the line sat, or how you knew when a detail was a saint and when it was a mayor. He bought another newspaper for the morning, folded it under his arm, and texted Marshall a single line: "Tomorrow I scan."

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: A 2018 study by Erica Boothby and colleagues found a liking gap: after a first conversation, people usually underestimate how much the other person liked them and enjoyed their company.
story:
Nicole got home at 9:40 and did not take off her coat for another six minutes. She stood in the hallway holding her phone, screen dark, and went over the whole evening again the way you run a thumb over a chipped tooth.

She had met Graham at the coffee place on Delancey at seven. She had arrived four minutes early and then pretended to study the menu board so she wouldn't look like someone waiting. When he came in, she'd waved with the hand that was holding her phone and nearly knocked her keys off the table. That was the first thing. The second thing was the story about her aunt's wedding, which she had started, lost the thread of, and abandoned mid-sentence with the words "you had to be there," though he had politely said he wished he had been. The third thing was the walk to the corner, twelve minutes of her talking about the chemistry set she'd wanted at nine years old, the one with the solutions that could ionize in water and turn things colors, and how her mother had said she'd burn the house down, and how she'd sulked about it for a month in a way she now described out loud as "petulant, honestly, indefensible." She had called herself petulant to a boy she was trying to impress. He had laughed. Was it a real laugh or a merciful one.

The doorbell rang at ten. Precious stood on the mat in her work polo, holding a paper bag of day-old bagels. "You have a face on," Precious said, pushing past her into the kitchen. "Rate it."

"I don't know yet. He hasn't texted."

"So it went bad."

"I don't know that either." Nicole finally hung her coat. The apartment felt very quiet, the way her grandmother's village in Kazakhstan had once felt when Nicole visited at eleven and stood at the edge of the steppe behind the house, the grass going on flat and unbroken until she couldn't tell where the land stopped being land.

Precious sat on the counter and split a bagel. "Okay, tell me the worst moment."

"I dumped half a sugar packet on my lap and said 'wow' to nobody."

"You're joking." Precious laughed so hard she had to put the bagel down. "Nicole. That's not bad, that's a highlight. What did he do?"

"He brushed it off the bench with his sleeve. His sleeve. Which means he touched my sugar."

"God." Precious pointed the bagel at her. "You know what we just read in Ms. Ricci's class? A study, 2018, Erica Boothby. People have a first conversation, and after, both of them underestimate how much the other one liked them. They call it the liking gap."

"That sounds like something people read to feel better."

"That's what I said and Ms. Ricci made me run the discussion anyway." Precious shrugged. "But think about it. He's probably home right now doing the exact thing you're doing, except about his own worst moment. What was his? He must have had one."

Nicole thought. There had been a moment when Graham was describing his brother and couldn't remember the word "kayak," and had drawn a paddling motion in the air, and gone pink. She'd filed it under charming, instantly, without deciding to. She had not filed her own sugar incident under anything so generous.

"It doesn't prove anything," Nicole said. "Even if the gap is real on average, he could be the exception. He could actually have hated it. An average doesn't cover one specific Tuesday."

"True," Precious said, mouth full. "Statistically that's fair."

"He kept checking his watch, maybe. Or he was just checking the time in a neutral way. I can't tell the difference anymore. I've replayed it so many times it's like a word you say until it stops meaning anything."

Precious hopped off the counter. "Okay, then stop doing the thing you can't do and do the thing you can. Text him something true and small. 'Had fun, your sleeve saved my sweater.' Something."

Nicole typed, deleted, typed. She settled on "thanks for sacrificing your sleeve to the sugar cause," sent it before she could weigh it further, and put the phone face-down on the table, which they both understood to be a temporary arrangement. They ate the bagels standing up. Precious told a story about a customer who had returned a bagel because it was "too round," and Nicole laughed with her whole chest, the kind of laugh she had not managed at the table with Graham, and noticed that, and filed it away.

The phone buzzed at 10:52. Nicole turned it over. Precious leaned in to read over her shoulder.

"okay confession," Graham had written. "I got home and told my brother I thought you were bored the entire time. he said did she say she was bored. I said no. he said then why do you think that. and I didn't have an answer. anyway. you weren't bored, right?"

Nicole stood very still. The liking gap, if that's what this was, had apparently been running in both directions the whole time, each of them certain the other was tolerating the evening. She thought about the study, about averages, about one specific Tuesday, about how knowing a thing was true in general didn't automatically make it true here, and how she was going to have to decide what to believe without proof either way. She started typing.

"not bored," she wrote. "I sugarboarded. different thing." She looked at Precious, who gave her a thumbs up with a bagel in her hand, and pressed send.

activity: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
knowledge_domain: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
fact: In the Jewish Passover tradition, the festive meal is called a Seder, a Hebrew word meaning 'order', because its rituals follow a fixed sequence from start to finish.
story:
The green book had been his grandfather's, and Christopher had told everyone he knew it by heart, which was true except for the parts he had never read. He sat on the low stone wall at the cemetery with the Haggadah open on his knees, Ria beside him eating sunflower seeds out of a paper bag, spitting shells into her cupped hand because the ground was not for littering, not here. His grandfather had led the Seder for forty-one years. Christopher had agreed to lead it this year in the hospital room, in April, when agreeing felt like a kindness rather than a job, and now the job was tomorrow and the kindness was a debt he could feel in his sternum.

"You look phlegmatic," Ria said. "Like a guy waiting for a bus."

"I'm prepared," he said. "Kadesh, Urchatz, Karpas. There's an order. It's literally called an order. Seder means order."

"Okay," Ria said, and cracked another seed.

His grandfather was under the flat marker with the pebbles people had left, dozens of them, small gray permissions to be visited. Christopher had not wanted to come today. His mother had suggested it in the voice she used under duress, tight and even, the voice that externalized nothing, and he had said sure, whatever, though he had actually wanted to say that talking to a stone was a thing he did not believe in, and then he had gone anyway, because saying no would have told her something about himself he was not ready to show.

The problem was the middle of the Seder. He knew the beginning, the way anyone knows a beginning: the blessing, the washing, the green vegetable dipped in salt water, his grandfather's voice going ragged at the part about bread of affliction. He knew the end, the songs, the cup for Elijah, the front door held open while the hallway went cold. It was the middle that failed him. When had the matzah get broken? Before the story or during it? Where did the sandw -- the sandwich, the Korech, the paste between two pieces, where exactly? He had practiced at his desk with index cards and the cards kept reordering themselves in the night like animals shifting in sleep.

Ria finished her seeds, wiped her palm on her jeans, and held out her hand. "Give me the cards."

"You don't know anything about this."

"I know you're going to breathe into a paper bag on Tuesday. Deal them out on the wall. If you can see it you can fix it."

They laid the fifteen steps along the stone in a row, Ria nudging them straight with one finger, Christopher crouching, moving Yachatz before Maggid, then after, then before again. "Why does it matter so much which one goes where," she said, not really asking, and he started to say because that's the whole point, and stopped, because the sentence rearranged itself as it left him. The meal was called an order because the rituals followed a fixed sequence, start to finish, and his grandfather had never once lost the place, not even last year, not even with the oxygen tube, when his voice came out in pieces and his hands shook over the cup. That was what Christopher wanted and could not say: not the words but the steadiness, the authority of a man who always knew what came next.

So he made it mechanical, which surprised him. He stopped trying to feel his way through and built a spine: the first cup, the washing, the vegetable, the breaking, the story, the second cup. Once the spine was there, the rest hung off it like clothes on a hook. Ria quizzed him, pointing at cards with a sunflower shell, and he got one wrong, and got it wrong again, and then got it right, and the rightness had a taste, metallic and clean.

He had told Ria he wasn't scared, and that was a lie, and he told her so out loud, standing up, dusting stone grit off his jeans. "I'm scared the whole thing is going to feel like a reading," he said. "Like a school thing. He made it feel like a table."

"Then don't perform it," Ria said. "Just do it in order and let the table be a table. That's literally what the word means. Order. You said so."

He put a pebble on the marker, a small one, gray like the others. Tomorrow there would be his mother's brisket and his cousins underfoot and his uncle's wine and the front door open to the cold hallway for a prophet who never visibly came, and Christopher would sit at the head of the table where the light fell, and say, "Kadesh," and see what his voice did.

He pocketed the cards. "Walk me out," he said. "You're on charoset duty."

activity: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
knowledge_domain: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
fact: London lies at about 51.5 degrees north, farther north than any point in the contiguous United States.
story:
Emilie spread the current map across the picnic table and weighted its corners with four flat stones from the fire pit. The paper had come from Mr. Bondarenko's box of teaching materials, the box he had carried up the trail and then left with the three of them while he walked down to the lake to check the fishing lines. Around the table the campsite smelled of cold ash and pine, and somewhere behind the tents a woodpecker worked at a dead trunk with patient, knocking regularity.

"Forty degrees, forty-five," Amna said, tracing the latitude lines with one finger. She was supposed to be finding the trade winds for their weather assignment, but she had drifted north instead, up along the Atlantic. "Emilie, look where London is."

Emilie leaned over. The map's grid was fine and the printing small, and at first she read the line wrong, because everyone read it wrong; that was the whole trouble. She put her finger on the little circle that marked the city and followed the dashed latitude line west across the ocean, across the folded crease, all the way to the coast of North America.

"It can't be up there," she said. "That's past the border."

"It isn't, though," Amna said. "Look at the numbers on the edge."

The numbers on the edge said fifty-one and a half. Emilie sat back on the bench and looked at the map without touching it, as if it might rearrange itself if she gave it room. London lay at about 51.5 degrees north, farther north than any point in the contiguous United States. She said it out loud once, slowly, testing it, and it still felt like a sentence in a language she could read but not quite speak. Ann, who had been slicing an apple into thin even wedges, set the knife down and came around the table to see for herself.

"So London is farther north than the whole US," Ann said. "Farther north than Maine. Farther north than the border."

"Than any point in the contiguous United States," Emilie said. "Yes. Which should mean it's frozen solid all winter, like Edmonton. Which it obviously isn't."

This was the assignment, though she hadn't understood that until this moment. Mr. Bondarenko had given them the current map and one question, written in his small blunt hand on an index card: explain why northern Europe is warmer than its latitude deserves. She had assumed the answer would be some fact to look up, a sentence to memorize, the kind of thing that ossifies into school knowledge overnight and then sits in you unchanged. Instead the answer was sitting on the table in front of her, and it was a shape.

"Here," she said, and put her finger in the Gulf of Mexico. She drew it east, then north, along the bright red band of warm water printed on the chart, the band that left the American coast and swung out across the Atlantic toward Europe. "The warm water goes this way. Look how it goes northeast, right at the latitude we were surprised about." She followed the red band to the latitude of London, then let her finger rest there. "If heat moves with the water, and the water moves here, then the heat moves here too."

"That's it?" Amna said. "A river in the ocean?"

"That's the shape of it, at least," Emilie said. "Whether that's the whole answer, I don't know."

Ann had gone quiet, turning an apple wedge in her fingers. "But the wind matters too," she said finally. "When we drove through the mountains last year, the weather came from the west, always from the west. The prevailing winds. So if the wind blows from the ocean onto the land, then the ocean's warmth gets carried inland." She looked up. "Currents and winds. It's both of them, isn't it."

Emilie had been ready to defend her single clean mechanism, and she felt the small stubborn impulse arrive and then, because Ann was probably right, let it go. She pulled the index card toward her and turned it over, and on the back Mr. Bondarenko had printed a second question, smaller: what else might you be missing? She laughed once, a short sound, mostly at herself.

"He knew we'd stop at the current," she said. "The ocean does the heating, and the wind is just, what, happenstance? No. The wind is the delivery system." She tapped the map. "The current loads the heat, and the wind carries it the last distance inland. Neither one works alone. That's a better answer than mine."

"Write it down before you decide it's wrong too," Amna said.

Emilie copied the map's grid onto a clean page of her notebook, then the red band, then the latitude line at 51.5, then the border of the United States far to the south of it. She wrote the two mechanisms side by side with the word "and" between them rather than "or." At the bottom of the page she added one more line: still uncertain how much each part contributes. It seemed more honest than a finished paragraph would have been.

Footsteps came up the trail, unhurried, accompanied by the clink of a creel. Mr. Bondarenko emerged from the trees with two small trout and the mild expression of a man who had expected nothing from the lake and been pleasantly surprised. He set the fish on the table's far edge, beside the apple cores, and looked at the notebook open beside the stones.

"We got it mostly," Emilie said, and turned the page toward him. "But the latitude thing is still strange to me. London, farther north than any point in the contiguous United States. I've seen that city in photographs my whole life and I always pictured it somewhere level with Oregon."

He looked at the page for a long moment, then at the map, then at her, and instead of answering he pointed at the fire pit with his chin. "Well," he said. "Get some wood on that. The current won't warm us tonight, and the wind is coming off the lake."

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: The secret printed ballot is called the Australian ballot because Australian colonies, Tasmania and Victoria, introduced it in 1856.
story:
The mock election had been Mr. Weiss's idea, and by third period it had descended into the particular ennui of seniors in October, the room heavy with fluorescent light and the smell of whiteboard marker. Eric had turned eighteen three weeks earlier, which meant that tonight, at the fire hall on Miller Street, he would vote for real. Mr. Weiss had printed gray sample ballots and set up a cardboard booth in the corner, and he was standing beside it now, arms crossed, waiting for someone to ask a question worth answering.

Lilia raised her hand. "Why does it have to be private? Like, why can't anybody watch you mark it?"

A few people shrugged. Someone said because it's your business, obviously, and Mr. Weiss didn't move, didn't nod, just let the answer sit there and go cold. "Eric," he said. "You're actually voting tonight. Want to take that one?"

Eric didn't want to. His father had opinions about this, loud ones, the kind shouted at the television, and Eric had spent two years not arguing back and not agreeing either, just absorbing it, and he didn't trust which voice would come out of his mouth. "I don't actually know why," he said. "I know it's called something. The way we do it. There's a name for it."

"Look it up," Mr. Weiss said, and tossed him the textbook.

Eric flipped through the elections chapter while Lilia watched over his shoulder. It wasn't in the body text, which was prolix enough to make his eyes slide, but he found it in the glossary, a short entry he read twice. "The Australian ballot," he said. "That's what it's called. The secret printed ballot." He kept his finger on the line. "It's named after Australia. Their colonies, Tasmania and Victoria, introduced it in 1856. We got it from them."

"So we borrowed it," Khushi said from the back row. "From a colony."

"A colony that was ahead of us," Lilia said, and something in the room shifted, the boredom thinning out, because for once the past had done something surprising.

Mr. Weiss still hadn't explained anything, which Eric understood was the whole method. "So think about the alternative," Mr. Weiss said. "What did voting look like before 1856?"

"Out loud," Eric said slowly, working it out as he said it. "Or with a colored ball you dropped in a jar. Everybody sees. Your landlord sees. Your boss sees." His father's voice was in his head again, the one that said voting should be public, that if you believed something you should stand up and say it, that secrecy was for cowards. And then there was Khushi's family, whose landlord had put a sign in the yard of their building, and Khushi had gone quiet about politics for a month. Two pictures of honesty, and Eric could not make them both true at once.

"People died for it not to be public," Lilia said. "That's in the chapter. People got fired. Beaten."

"Or people lie in public and vote honest in private," Khushi said. "My uncle says that's how it works where he grew up. You tell the loud man what he wants to hear, then you go vote."

Mr. Weiss assigned the mock vote. One at a time they went behind the cardboard booth, and Eric noticed that even here, in a classroom where nothing counted, everyone folded their ballot before handing it to the counter, even Khushi, even Lilia, even the boy who had spent all period announcing his opinions. The secrecy had already gotten into them, instinct without argument.

That evening his father drove him to the fire hall and waited in the car, engine running. Inside, the line was short. A woman with a clipboard found Eric's name, and a volunteer led him to a machine with a curtain, and the volunteer said, "First time? Nobody's allowed to see how you mark it. That's the whole point." Eric stood at the machine transfixed by the smallness of it, the little levers and the dim bulb, the entire apparatus of the Australian ballot, borrowed from Tasmania and Victoria in 1856, assembled here in a fire hall in Ohio so that a person could be alone with a decision.

He thought about his father in the parking lot, believing Eric would vote his way, and about Khushi's uncle, and about standing up for things out loud. He pulled the curtain shut. He did not decide until the pencil was actually in his hand, and even then, marking it, he could not have said he was certain, only that it was his, made alone, and folded twice before anyone could see. When he came out, his father leaned across and pushed the passenger door open.

"Well?" his father said. "Who'd you vote for?"

Eric pulled the seatbelt across his chest and clicked it. "Drive," he said.

activity: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
knowledge_domain: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
fact: The Limits to Growth, published in 1972 for the Club of Rome by an MIT team, used a computer model called World3 to link population, food, industry, pollution and resources.
story:
The county water office smelled of instant coffee and old carpet, and Laurie had been given a desk between the copier and a filing cabinet marked DO NOT TRUST. Her internship was supposed to be two weeks of filing aquifer reports, but on the second morning Ms. Takahashi, the hydrologist whose office this technically was, slid a binder across the table and said the town council wanted a model. "They approved four hundred new units off Route 9," she said. "They want to know what that does to the water. I want you to build them something honest."

"Something honest" turned out to mean a spreadsheet, and by lunch Laurie had eleven columns and no idea how they talked to each other. Population grew, pumping grew, the aquifer dropped, but the drop made the wells cost more, and the cost slowed the building, and the building was what the council wanted, so none of it moved in a straight line. Katrina, who had wrangled her way into the same internship by claiming experience she did not have, leaned over the divider. "You look like you're trying to resuscitate a dead frog," she said. "Also, I found the good coffee, it's in the cabinet Ms. Takahashi thinks nobody opens."

Bastien arrived at three, dropped his bike helmet on the copier, and announced he had spent his lunch at the historical society being held hostage by the town's last great raconteur, a retired selectman who could stretch the flood of 1978 into forty minutes. "But he said something useful, sort of," Bastien said. "He said there was a report, way back, that tried to do what you're doing. Not for our town. For the whole world. He couldn't remember the name of it, only that it made people furious."

Laurie found it on the office's ancient desktop while Katrina narrated the search like a sports announcer. It was called The Limits to Growth, published in 1972 for the Club of Rome, and an MIT team had written it. "It's not just arguments," she said, scrolling. "They built a computer model. It's called World3." Ms. Takahashi passed behind them with her coffee and said only, "Mm," which Laurie was learning meant keep going.

The model linked things. Population, food, industry, pollution, resources. Laurie read the list twice, then sat very still, because that was her spreadsheet. Hers was smaller and stupider, one aquifer instead of a planet, but the shape was the same: everything touching everything, so that you couldn't pull one thread without feeling the whole cloth move. "That's why my columns won't behave," she said. "I kept trying to solve them one at a time."

"They became bellicose when you tried that," Katrina agreed. "Like geese."

Bastien had his own project, which he explained while stacking his helmet inside itself for no reason: he wanted the council's presentation to include a slide of the old swim hole, the one that had gone dry in his grandfather's time when the first subdivision went in. "Numbers don't move them," he said. "Pictures of dead swim holes might. I want people to feel it in the gut." Laurie said that was manipulation, and Bastien said yes, obviously, that was the point, and Katrina said they were both right and both insufferable.

They worked until the overhead lights came on automatically and made everything yellow. Laurie built loops into her model: new houses, more demand, deeper pumping, higher cost, slower growth, then growth anyway because the council could rezone. She ran it and the aquifer dipped, recovered a little when a conservation ordinance kicked in, dipped again. There was no clean answer, which she understood was itself the answer, though not one the council would frame and hang on a wall. At some point she noticed Bastien had quietly made his slide, and it was good, the swim hole gray and cracked, a child's rubber boot in the mud, and she hated a little how well it worked on her.

Ms. Takahashi read the printout standing up, one hand on the filing cabinet. "You've made a small World3," she said. "Yours has one town in it instead of the whole globe, and your pollution is just nitrates, but it's the same idea wearing different clothes." She looked at Laurie over the page. "The council won't like it. They'll ask which number to change so the answer comes out yes."

"Which number does come out yes?" Laurie asked.

"None of them alone," Ms. Takahashi said. "That's the part that took me twenty years to stop resenting."

On the last day, the council chamber was too cold and the chairs were the folding kind that pinch. Katrina whispered that the vice chair had fallen asleep at a sewer hearing once, a fact she had collected the way she collected everything. Laurie presented the loops, the dips, the recovery that was never quite a recovery, and Bastien followed with the boot in the mud. The vice chair woke up for the slide. Then a councilor in a gray suit said the town had always grown and always would, and another said the aquifer had never failed them yet, and Laurie understood that both statements were true and neither one was a reason.

Afterward, in the parking lot, the light going amber over the Route 9 fields where the four hundred units would go, Bastien said, "We didn't win." Katrina said, "We didn't lose, either, they tabled it till fall, that's like a draw with extra steps." Laurie zipped her binder into her bag, the loops still in it, the numbers still tangled in each other the way the report said the whole world was tangled, one small version of a much older problem, and she said, "Run it again Monday. I want to see what happens if the ordinance starts a year earlier."

"Of course you do," Katrina said, and unlocked her bike.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The Stanley Cup, donated in 1892 by Lord Stanley of Preston and first awarded in 1893, is the oldest existing trophy awarded to a professional sports team in North America.
story:
My grandfather's recliner has a torn seam on the left armrest, and if anyone else sits in it during a playoff game, the whole household agrees, we lose. I have believed this for as long as I have believed anything, which is to say I never examined it. Tonight the house is loud, my uncle obstreperous after his third beer, my mother shushing him with one eye on the hallway where my grandmother is supposedly sleeping. Hamzah and Gregoire are on the floor with their phones face down, an act of faith they both regard as enormous. Mr. Rosen from next door has let himself in through the back door, as he does, holding a plate of lemon squares and looking slightly ashamed of his timing.

I should say now that I am not a reliable witness to this evening. I proved that to myself only afterwards, and I will try to tell it the way it actually happened rather than the way I first told Hamzah it happened, which had me calm and wise and utterly wrong about the score.

The game is game seven, which everyone knows is the only game that matters, and by the second period we are down by one and the room has gone quiet in that particular way a loud room goes quiet, all at once, like a held breath. To fill the silence, because I cannot stand it, I start talking about the trophy itself. "You know it's the oldest existing trophy awarded to a professional sports team in North America," I say. "The Stanley Cup. Lord Stanley of Preston donated it in 1892, and it was first awarded in 1893. Everything else, all the other trophies, came after."

Gregoire asks how I know that, and the honest answer is that I looked it up this afternoon, which is also when I learned I had been wrong for years. In the fourth grade I did a presentation on hockey and told the class, with total confidence, that the Cup was first awarded in 1903. Mr. Rosen, who was substituting that day, had said nothing. Tonight he says, mildly, "You've done your homework since." There is no accusation in it, but I feel one anyway, a small cold foreboding that has nothing to do with hockey.

Here is what I keep coming back to, though, the thing I cannot make lie flat. My grandfather, before he died two winters ago, used to tell a story about the 1962 final, how he watched it in this living room as a boy, sitting in that same recliner, and how his own father said the chair was lucky because his grandfather had sat in it for the 1931 final too. I loved that story because it made the chair a kind of inheritance, a place where watching became something you did on behalf of the dead. When I was nine, and the team went to the final that year, I sat in the recliner for all seven games and we lost the last one in double overtime, and afterward my mother said, quietly, that maybe luck was not the right frame for any of this.

After the second intermission I recalibrate. I decide that my job tonight is not to believe in the chair but to be the person in the room who knows things, who can say when a team has pulled its goalie or why the faceoff matters, and so I keep talking, and Hamzah keeps grinning at me like he can see the machinery of my coping. When we tie it early in the third, my uncle stands up so fast he knocks over his beer, and my mother appears with towels, and Gregoire starts a chant that dies of embarrassment halfway through, and for a minute the room is pure noise, no history in it at all.

We lose in the last ninety seconds. A turnover at the blue line, a shot through a screen, and the net ripples and the room makes a sound I have never heard a room make before, a single syllable of grief from eight people at once. Mr. Rosen sets down his lemon squares. Hamzah puts his hand flat on the carpet as if steadying the floor.

And here is the twist, which I did not see coming and which rearranged the whole evening for me. Cleaning up afterwards, carrying the plate to the kitchen, I found my grandmother standing at the counter in her nightgown, awake the whole time. She heard the goal. She said, "Your grandfather made that story up, you know. The 1931 part. He bought that chair in 1960 at an auction, and his grandfather was dead before he ever sat in it." She took the plate from my hands. "He liked the idea of it more than the fact of it," she said. "I never had the heart to argue."

I stood there recalibrating everything again, the chair, the luck, the story I would tell Hamzah tomorrow, the fact I had gotten wrong in the fourth grade and corrected and been smug about tonight, all of it tangled together with a loss that still hurt in my chest. I could hold two things at once, I thought: that the chair was just a chair, and that my grandfather's invention had been its own kind of true. What I could not do was decide whether that made the lying worse or better, and I went to bed with the question unresolved, the television downstairs murmuring highlights to an empty room.

In the morning I moved the recliner's cushion aside to vacuum, and underneath, pressed into the springs, I found a folded score sheet in my grandfather's handwriting, dated 1962, game four, and a note in pencil that said, Tell them the chair is older than this. I sat down on the armrest, the torn one, and read it twice more.

"Grandma," I called toward the kitchen. "Come look at this."

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
knowledge_domain: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
fact: A few drops of water in melted chocolate can make it seize into a thick, grainy paste, because the sugar and cocoa particles clump together.
story:
The market opened at seven, and by seven fifteen Autumn had already broken one rule of Mr. Chukwu's stall: she had touched the display truffles with her bare fingers, leaving little moons of heat on the dark shells. "You want to sell people a mirror, not a fingerprint," he said, not unkindly, and handed her a cloth. He sold chocolates next to the honey people and the tomato people, and he had agreed, after three Saturdays of her hovering, to teach her to temper.

Ziyad had come along because the market had free samples of cheese, and Maude had come because Ziyad had, though she claimed it was for the peaches. They arranged themselves on stools behind the stall while Mr. Chukwu set up the double boiler, water murmuring below, the bowl of chopped couverture balanced above it like something asleep. He explained nothing at length. He said only that the chocolate had to melt, then cool, then be held at a temperature where it behaved, and that Autumn's job was to watch and stir. "Watching is a skill," he said. "Most people look the way a cat looks at a wall."

She stirred slowly, feeling the chocolate loosen from chips into something glossy and continuous. Maude leaned in and said it looked like a river in an advertisement, and Ziyad said it looked like a sauce his mother made, and both of these, Autumn thought, were ways of not saying what she actually felt, which was that the bowl seemed alive under her spoon. Mr. Chukwu had a theory about patience, some mild asceticism of the hands, no scraping, no hurrying, no doubling the heat because you were bored. She was trying to practice it. She was sixteen and not naturally gifted at austerity.

The problem arrived as steam. She lifted the bowl to show Maude how it flowed off the spoon, and when she set it back, condensation from the rim of the boiler flicked upward. A few drops, no more, kissed the surface of the chocolate. She stirred, and the spoon suddenly dragged. The bowl that had been a river was now a thick, grainy paste, stiff and dull, gripping the spoon like cement. She looked at Mr. Chukwu, expecting anger, and got instead a small shrug that was worse than anger, because it meant the mistake was ordinary.

"That's seized," said Maude, who had spent the previous night reading chocolate forums for reasons she did not explain. "A few drops of water in melted chocolate and it does that. The sugar and cocoa particles clump together." Ziyad said this was the most acerbic thing chocolate had ever done to anyone, which wasn't quite the right use of the word, but nobody corrected him. Autumn stared into the bowl. She had done everything with attention. She had watched like a cat watching a wall, and still a few invisible drops had undone an hour.

"So it's ruined," she said. "All of it." Mr. Chukwu scraped the seized mass into a container and labeled it for ganache, where, he said, cream would make the clumping irrelevant, since you were adding water on purpose, in quantity, from the start. That was the part Autumn kept turning over while she chopped a new batch. The same ingredient, water, was a catastrophe in drops and a technique in cups. It seemed unfair, and then it seemed like something else, a kind of logic she could almost hold. She had always wanted rules that worked like math. This one worked more like a conversation, where the meaning of a word depended on who said it and how much of it there was.

She began again with the second batch, and this time she interpolated her own step between his instructions: she wiped the rim of the boiler dry every few minutes, and she moved the bowl off the heat whenever she lifted the spoon to test the drip. It was not in any recipe. It was what she had learned from the first failure, grafted onto what he had taught her, and she could not have said which part mattered more. Ziyad pronounced the new batch "less murdery." Maude held a dipped strawberry up to the light and said nothing at all, which from Maude was applause.

When the chocolate cooled on the marble slab, it set with a shine like wet stone, and when Autumn broke a strip off the edge it snapped, a clean sound that made Ziyad flinch and then laugh. Mr. Chukwu took a piece, snapped it near his ear, and ate it without comment, which was his version of a diploma. She still did not know whether she could do it again tomorrow, or whether the next humid morning would betray her the way the steam had. She dipped one more strawberry, wiped the rim of the boiler, and set the strip of chocolate down where the early sun crossed the table. "Snap it again," she said. "I want to hear it."

activity: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
knowledge_domain: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
fact: In Kazuo Ishiguro's 1989 novel The Remains of the Day, the butler Stevens reports events accurately but misreads their meaning, including his own feelings.
story:
Ms. Chukwu had written one question on the board before the bell finished ringing: can a narrator tell you everything and still fool you? Xavier copied it into his notebook, then underlined it twice, because he had decided over the weekend that he would be the one to answer it. He had read The Remains of the Day in two sittings, and he had a theory.

"The butler is lying," he said, before she had even finished arranging the handouts. "Stevens. He says he wasn't in love with Miss Kenton, so he's lying. That's the trick. Unreliable narrator, case closed." He heard himself say it and liked the sound of it, the confidence of it. Ayan, beside him, made a low noise that could have been agreement or a cough.

Thalie turned around in her seat. "Go back to the evening his father dies," she said. "He's serving drinks upstairs while the old man is dying downstairs. He writes that it was his finest moment, that dignity meant everything that night. Every fact is right there. The guests, the wine, the exact hour. He doesn't hide any of it."

"So he's honest," Xavier said.

"He's honest and wrong," Thalie said. "That's what got me. What he says he felt doesn't match what he did. He spends three pages on Miss Kenton's crying, on her hand on his shoulder, and he files all of it under staff management."

Ms. Chukwu said nothing. She had a way of standing very still near the window that made the room feel like it was waiting, and Xavier, who liked answers better than questions, felt the waiting press on him.

He turned back to the book, flipping pages while Ayan watched. There was the moment Stevens claimed he was merely tired, merely in need of rest, and then Ishiguro showed him weeping in front of strangers at a bus stop, unable to say why. There was the drive to the west country that Stevens called a staff-plan problem, a matter of rearranging personnel, while every mile of it was longing dressed in a collar and tie. The book was from 1989, Ms. Chukwu had told them, written decades after the world it described, and Xavier began to see that the distance was the point. Stevens had had a whole life to rehearse the account, and the rehearsal had made the facts accurate and the meaning rotten. He tried to metabolize this, to break it down into something usable, and found it would not break down cleanly. The old adage about actions speaking louder than words was too simple here, because the words were not lies. They were something worse, something with no easy name, and the namelessness was what the whole novel was built on.

"Okay," he said finally, and his voice came out quieter than he intended. "I was wrong. He's not lying. He reports everything, and the reporting is exact. But he misreads what it means, even his own feelings. You can't catch him on a single fact. You have to catch him on the whole shape." Saying it, he understood how much heavier that was than his first answer. A liar you can expose. A man who has fooled himself leaves you nothing to expose, only the gap between the record and the truth.

"So how do you ever trust anyone?" Ayan asked, half laughing. "If someone can be accurate and wrong at the same time?"

"You trust what they do," Thalie said. "But even that."

"Even that," Xavier agreed. He thought, briefly, of the letter he had written to his father last month, the one that said he wasn't angry about the move, that he understood the job came first, that they could talk whenever. Every fact in the letter was true. The job had come first. He was still deciding what the letter had meant.

Ms. Chukwu finally moved from the window and began handing out the assignment sheet. "Your essay," she said, "will be on point of view and trust. Four pages. I want you to choose one narrator and show how the telling shapes what we believe." Xavier took his copy and read the first line, which said that secondary or ancillary characters may be used as evidence but may not be your central subject. His subject was already chosen, the butler, the whole route of it clear in his head.

"Xavier," Ms. Chukwu said, pausing at his desk. "You argued very persuasively today. For the first five minutes."

"Which five are you grading?"

"The last ones," she said, and moved on down the row.

activity: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
knowledge_domain: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
fact: Between two parallel charged plates, the electric field strength equals the voltage across them divided by the distance between them, written E = V/d.
story:
The gymnasium smelled of hot glue and orange soda, and Payton's capacitor was already misbehaving. She had built it from two sheets of aluminum foil taped to opposite sides of a shoebox, a 9-volt battery clipped to each sheet, and a small foam ball suspended on thread between them, which was supposed to sway toward the negative plate and demonstrate, in one graceful gesture, everything she had spent three weeks learning. Instead the ball hung plumb still, indifferent, as though physics were a rumor it had not heard.

"You could just poke it," said Reilly, who had abandoned her own table, a display about lichen that climbs montane tree lines, to come watch Payton suffer. "Nobody would know."

"Mr. Lawson would know. He notices everything. He once marked me down for a crooked staple."

Across the gym, a baking-soda volcano erupted for the fourth time, and a knot of freshmen erupted with it. Raphaelle, its creator, stood in the fine white mist of her own triumph while the freshmen lionized her like a visiting celebrity, taking photos, asking for autographs on their programs. Payton watched the foam ball do nothing and thought, without bitterness, that lava was easy.

Mr. Lawson arrived at her table holding his clipboard like a man holding a verdict. "So," he said. "Tell me what's happening between those plates."

"An electric field," Payton said, and then, because that felt like a coupon and not a purchase, she kept going. "Between two parallel charged plates, the field strength equals the voltage across them divided by the distance between them." She pointed at the shoebox, at the battery label, at her ruler. "So mine is 9 volts over 4 centimeters. E equals V over d."

"Numerically?"

She did it on the corner of her poster, then said it out loud: 225 volts per centimeter, which sounded enormous and was making her doubt herself. Mr. Lawson neither nodded nor frowned, which was his version of a poker face, and wrote something down. Then he asked the question she had been dreading. "And what is the ball telling you?"

"Nothing," she admitted. "That's the part I can't figure out."

He said, "Judging resumes at two," and moved on to the volcanologist.

Payton sat on the folded bleachers behind her table with Reilly and ate half a granola bar that was mostly oats of despair. "I measured the gap wrong," she said at last. "I measured plate to plate, outside the box, but I taped the foil down in the middle of each side, so the real gap is smaller. Three centimeters, maybe less. Smaller d means a stronger field, so the field is stronger than I calculated, which means the ball should move, which means the ball isn't the problem." Reilly raised an eyebrow. "The charge is the problem. The foil's touching the tape, the tape's insulating it, the plates barely hold anything. V isn't really 9. It's almost nothing."

"So fix it," Reilly said, in the tone of someone pointing out that rain falls downward.

Raphaelle wandered over during her victory lap, still dusted with sodium bicarbonate, and offered commentary. "You know what my volcano taught me? Drama works. People like a diminuendo." She wiggled her fingers downward. "The eruption fades out, everyone leans in. Your ball just sits there. Make it fade in."

Payton took this as seriously as it deserved, which was about forty percent, and rebuilt the capacitor on the folding table with Raphaelle holding the tape and Reilly reciting the lichen facts she was supposed to be presenting instead. This time she bent the foil tabs so they gripped the battery terminals directly, and she shaved the gap down to a clean 2 centimeters with fresh plates, and she wrote the new math on the poster before she even tested it, because she wanted the calculation to be a prediction and not an excuse. "9 over 2," she murmured. "450 volts per centimeter. Doubled the field by halving the distance."

"Do you feel powerful?" Raphaelle asked.

"Territorial," said Payton, and connected the battery.

The foam ball swung sideways and stuck to the negative plate like a small white flag of surrender, then, when she disconnected the clip, drifted back to center in a slow diminuendo of thread and static, exactly as Raphaelle had prescribed. Mr. Lawson came back at two, looked at the ball, looked at the corrected arithmetic, and wrote something longer on his clipboard than he had before. "And if I moved the plates farther apart without changing the battery?"

"Weaker field," Payton said. "Same voltage, bigger d, so V over d gets smaller. I'd have to show you." She picked up the ruler, grinning. "Move them yourself if you want. I'll watch the ball."

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: Many food banks cannot accept home-cooked or opened food, because they cannot check how it was prepared or stored.
story:
The food bank operated out of the library's basement on Saturdays, between the large-print section and a mural of a whale reading to children, which struck Mackenzie as either charming or deeply strange depending on the hour. She had signed up because her mother had said volunteering would look good on applications, and because applications were now behind her, she had almost cancelled. She came anyway, wearing her older sneakers, and was handed a hairnet by a woman named Poppy who treated the hairnet as though it were a beret.

"You're the high school one," Poppy said. "Emrick's the other one. He's reorganizing the cans by mood."

"By what?"

"By mood. Tomato paste is having a hard week, apparently." Emrick waved from the shelf, a tall boy with the deliberate slowness of someone who had learned that moving quickly got you assigned more work.

The morning was mostly boxes. Mackenzie learned the intake table quickly: check dates, check seals, sort canned things into canned things, boxed into boxed. There was a laminated sheet taped to the table with the rules, and she read it twice while Poppy quizzed her with the seriousness of a customs officer. Sealed, unopened, labeled. She had just begun to feel competent when a woman she recognized came down the stairs holding a casserole dish wrapped in a tea towel.

It was her neighbor from four doors down, the one who blow-dried her dog on the porch in summer. The dish, from the smell of it, was lasagna, still warm.

"I made too much," the neighbor said, setting it on the table like an offering. "It seemed a shame, with all you do down here."

Mackenzie looked at the lasagna. She looked at the laminated sheet. Behind it, Poppy had gone very still, the way people do when they are watching someone about to touch a wet paint sign. The rule was there in plain print, and Mackenzie understood it as she read it aloud, slowly, enunciating each clause because she hated how it sounded and hoped that saying it carefully would make it sound less like rejection. Most food banks couldn't accept home-cooked or opened food. They had no way to check how it was prepared or stored, so anything without a sealed, commercial label had to be turned away, no matter how good it smelled, and this one smelled genuinely excellent.

"I'm so sorry," Mackenzie said. "I can't take it. It's not that I doubt your lasagna. I bet your lasagna is the best thing in this entire basement, including the whale."

The neighbor laughed, but her hands stayed on the dish a moment longer. "My mother used to say food is how you say the thing you can't say." She lifted it back up. "Some aphorism, huh. I'll drop it at the shelter on Miller Street. They do a hot meal, they can use it."

After she left, Mackenzie sat with the exchange the way one sits with a stone in a shoe. Emrick drifted over, ostensibly to shelve a can of beets, actually to spectate. "Rough," he offered.

"It's a stupid rule and a good rule at the same time," Mackenzie said. "I'm certain it's both. What I'm not certain about is what I'm supposed to feel about that."

"That's very first-year-of-college of you."

"Shut up. You organized beans by mood."

"By mood," Emrick said, wounded. "It's different."

Poppy called them back to work, and the afternoon resumed its shape: boxes, dates, seals, the low library hum of the ceiling fans and, faintly, through the floor, someone upstairs failing quietly at a computer. A disaffected teenager had been sighing at the printers since noon, and every sigh drifted down through the vents like a weather report from another country. Mackenzie sorted. She thought about her neighbor carrying the lasagna back up the stairs, warm dish, cold fact, and how the rule protected people she would never meet from risks she couldn't see, and how it also told a woman with a tea towel that her kindness was not a currency the table accepted. Both of those were true. Neither one cancelled the other. She had expected, somewhere in eighteen years of being handed positions to hold, that careful thinking would eventually deliver her a single clean conclusion, and instead it had delivered her a lasagna she could smell and could not take.

Near closing, Mr. Qureshi, the librarian, came down with a box of donation flyers and paused at the intake table. He noticed the laminated sheet, peered at it, and nodded slowly, a man discovering that the basement had laws.

"Turning things away nicely," he observed, "is harder than taking them."

"I'm getting better at it," Mackenzie said, and reached for the next box.

activity: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
knowledge_domain: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
fact: The Taylor rule, proposed by economist John Taylor, says that when inflation rises one percentage point a central bank should raise its interest rate by more than one percentage point.
story:
The automatic doors exhaled warm air at Charlotte as she followed her mother into the grocery store, a stack of index cards rubber-banded in her coat pocket. On one side of each card was an economics term she needed for Thursday's club debate; on the other, a biology definition for the exam she had the same week. She had drawn the cards at random, which was why "speciation," the splitting of one species into two, now lived next to "inflation," and her brain kept trying to file them together.

She pushed the cart down the cereal aisle while her mother went for onions. The debate topic was whether the central bank should raise interest rates at all this year, and Jeff had cornered her after last week's meeting to say the whole thing was simpler than everyone pretended. If prices were rising by a percentage point more, you raised the rate by a percentage point more. Match it, cancel it out, go home. He had said it with such certainty that she had nodded along, and only in the parking lot afterward did the nodding start to bother her, the way a smooth answer can captivate you exactly long enough to stop you checking it.

Simone found her by the oatmeal, holding her phone and a jar of peanut butter she had no intention of buying. "Ms. Joseph said you're arguing against Jeff," she said.

"I'm supposed to be. I don't actually know if he's wrong."

"He's wrong." Simone set the jar down among the oatmeal. "Remember when I missed the meeting and had to get everything from Ben? He went on about the Taylor rule for ten minutes."

"What is it, actually? Ben sends me slides with no words on them."

"It's John Taylor's rule. When inflation goes up one percentage point, the bank should raise the interest rate by more than one percentage point."

"More," Charlotte repeated, and stood there while a man reached past her for the store brand. More than matching. Not equal, more. She turned an index card over in her mind and could not make Jeff's arithmetic sit next to Simone's sentence. "Why more?"

"That's the part Ben didn't say, and I didn't ask, and I've been too embarrassed to admit it for a week." Simone looked genuinely miserable, which somehow made Charlotte feel better. "But the number part, that I'm sure of. One point in, more than one point out."

They walked toward the dairy, Charlotte steering the cart, Simone reading the cereal prices like they were a stock ticker. Charlotte tried saying it aloud. "So if prices start climbing faster, the bank doesn't just keep pace, it leans harder than the climb." She liked the shape of that, but liking the shape of a sentence was not the same as understanding it, and she had made that mistake before, in English class, with an essay about a book she had not finished. "I can argue it without knowing why it's more. Is that lying?"

"It's citing," Simone said. "There's a difference, but it's thin."

Her mother appeared at the end of the aisle with onions and a look that meant she had been standing there long enough to hear some of it. "Are you two doing homework in the store?"

"Economics," Charlotte said, which was true and also a small hiding of the fact that she was enjoying it, that the store had turned into somewhere she could think out loud, the fluorescent hum like white noise over the argument running in her head.

At the checkout, unloading yogurt and bread, she worked the index cards out of her pocket and spread three of them on the divider bar. Inflation, interest rates, and, stubbornly, speciation, which refused to become economics no matter how she looked at it. Two things that had been one thing, splitting into two things that could no longer be confused with each other. She thought about Jeff's position and her own, drifting apart over a single percentage point, becoming distinguishable. Maybe that was a stretch. She put the card back.

At the register she said, "Thursday, I'm going to open with the Taylor rule and admit I can defend the number but not the reason behind it. Let Jeff explain why matching isn't enough, if he can."

"He'll hate that," Simone said, digging for her bus fare.

"I know." The cashier slid the yogurt across the scanner, and Charlotte picked up the cards one by one, squaring their edges against the counter. "He'll hate that more than losing."

activity: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
knowledge_domain: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
fact: Simone de Beauvoir's The Second Sex, published in 1949, contains the line usually translated as 'one is not born, but rather becomes, a woman', arguing that society shapes womanhood.
story:
Coralie had taped the passage from Jane Eyre to the wall of the reading nook, between the window and the shelf where her mother kept the novels nobody reread. Bertha Mason's introduction, the part where Mr. Rochester explains his mad wife in the attic, and beneath it in her own handwriting: property? madness? who gets to say? She had promised Tala and Cheyanne she would have a position by Thursday, because Ms. Hassan's assignment demanded one, and because Coralie hated having no position more than she hated being wrong.

Tala arrived first, carrying the Marxist handout Ms. Hassan had photocopied, already dog-eared. Cheyanne came twenty minutes late with iced coffee and the announcement that she had read the whole Brontë section again at midnight and thought Rochester was worse than she'd thought at midnight the previous week. They folded themselves into the nook, Cheyanne on the floor with her back against the baseboard, Tala cross-legged on the cushion Coralie's grandmother had embroidered with peacocks.

"Okay," Tala said. "Capitalism first. Rochester owns the house, the wife, the narrative. Bertha is collateral damage on his balance sheet. That's the whole paragraph."

"But the feminist lens doesn't just reduce to money," Cheyanne said, stirring her melting ice with the straw. "Jane wants to be chosen, not kept. She refuses to be a mistress even when it costs her everything she wants."

"Exactly," Tala said. "Even when it costs her everything she wants. Whose wanting is that, though? She's trained to want a wedding or nothing. There's no third door."

Coralie had been quiet, which was unlike her, and both of them had noticed. She pulled her grandmother's copy of The Second Sex down from the shelf, the 1949 book she'd found there in September and carried around for a week like contraband. She opened it to the page she'd flagged with a receipt from the pharmacy. "Listen," she said, and read the line aloud: "One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman."

Cheyanne stopped stirring. "That's de Beauvoir?"

"That's de Beauvoir. Society shapes womanhood, is the argument. So Jane's refusal isn't just Jane's. It's what her century taught a woman of her class to count as virtue."

"So then nobody's choices are anybody's," Tala said, though not unkindly. She was the one of them who argued like she was tightening a bolt, small turns, testing. "If wanting is trained, then Rochester's trained too, and Bertha's madness is trained, and we've exculpated everyone in the novel and learned nothing."

"I didn't say exculpate," Coralie said. "I said trace." But even as she said it she felt the ground shift, because Tala was right that the two lenses pulled against each other. Marxism wanted Rochester accountable as a man with power; the feminist lens wanted to ask why the women kept apologizing for existing inside his power. The encapsulation she'd written in her notebook that morning, both lenses agree the attic is not an accident, suddenly looked too clean, a bow on top of something that refused to be wrapped.

Cheyanne leaned her head back against the wall. "My mom read this book at my age and thought Jane was brave. Now I think Jane is brave and trapped at the same time and I can't get those apart."

"That's allowed," Coralie said. "That might be the position."

Ms. Hassan appeared at four with a plate of lemon squares, because she was the neighbour before she was the teacher and had never learned to arrive without food. She set the plate on the windowsill and asked what they'd decided, and Coralie started to give her the tidy answer and stopped. "Rochester is a landowner disposing of people like assets. Jane is a woman whose idea of freedom was shaped by the world that limited her. I can hold both. What I can't tell yet is whether Jane's leaving was hers."

Ms. Hassan took a lemon square and ate it without comment, which was the most obstreperous thing she could have done, since it left the problem entirely theirs. Cheyanne laughed at the look on Coralie's face.

After Ms. Hassan went back through the hedge, Tala read the de Beauvoir line again, twice, out loud, as if checking whether it would still be true the second time. Coralie uncapped her pen and wrote at the bottom of the taped page: one is not born, but rather becomes, a woman, and after it, in smaller letters: so which parts of me are mine? She looked at the question for a long moment, then left it there, unanswered, taped beside Bertha in her attic, and handed the pen to Cheyanne. "Your turn. Add what you'd argue."

Cheyanne took the pen and held it over the paper without writing.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: A guitar in standard tuning has its six strings tuned, from lowest to highest, to E, A, D, G, B and E.
story:
The guitar had lived in the hall closet for so long that Rose had stopped seeing it, the way you stop seeing a coat rack. It belonged to her grandfather, who had died in March, and when her mother finally pulled it out and leaned it against the living room wall, Rose found herself circling it all evening like the whole thing might go off.
