The strings were dull, the wood smelled faintly of dust and old cigarettes, and when she pressed the lowest string down behind a fret and plucked it, the note sagged somewhere below where it should have been. She didn't know how she knew that. She just knew.

She had watched videos all summer without ever touching an instrument, so her knowledge was entirely theoretical, which she suspected was a way of not learning anything at all. Now, with September coming and college after that, she wanted one thing she could do with her hands. She wanted it so specifically that it embarrassed her, so she told no one except Londyn, who came over the next afternoon with her bike helmet still on and said, "Okay, show me the mystery grandpa guitar."

Rose sat on the floor with the guitar across her lap and her phone open to a tuning app she'd downloaded at two in the morning. "It says the strings should be, from lowest to highest, E, A, D, G, B, and E," she said. "Two E's. I thought that was a typo at first." Londyn crouched next to her, helmet under her arm, and watched the little needle on the screen waver. Rose turned the tuning peg at the head of the low string, a quarter turn, then less, then barely anything at all, and the needle crept toward center. The string tightened under her fingers with a faint creak, like a door deciding to open. When the needle finally steadied, the note rang out clean and low, and Rose felt something in her chest settle with it.

"That one E is at the bottom and the other is at the top," Londyn said. "Like bookends."

"Except it's not the same E," Rose said. "The top one is way higher. Same letter, different note." She moved to the next string, twisting and plucking, twisting and plucking, and the guitar began to sound like a guitar instead of a rumor of one. Somewhere around the fourth string she got careless and turned the peg too far, and the note climbed past where it belonged, sharp and thin. She had to bring it back down. It occurred to her that tuning was mostly the art of going too far and then apologizing.

Rogan arrived mid-afternoon with a bag of cherries and the news that their neighbor, Mr. Müller, had once played in a band, which Rose's mother confirmed with suspicious speed. Within the hour Mr. Müller was standing in their living room with his hands in his pockets, refusing to touch the guitar. "It's yours now," he said. "You tune it, you learn it. I'll listen." So Rose went back to work with an audience, and her hands, which had been steady all afternoon, began to betray her. She turned a peg the wrong way and the B string went loose and wrong, and Rogan said, kindly, "Wrong direction," and Rose flushed to her ears.

"You're allowed to be bad at this," Londyn told her, and Rose said, "I know that," and then, quieter, "except I don't actually believe it." She found the pitch again, brought the needle home, and moved to the last string, the high E, the twin of the one she'd started with. When all six were done she strummed them open, once, all together. The chord was strange and open, not really a song, but it was in tune, every string agreeing with every other one, and the three of them sat there in the ringing.

Later, walking Rogan out, Rose admitted what she'd been thinking. "I spent all summer reading about how to practice. Efficient methods, spaced repetition, metacognition, all of it. And I think I was reading so I wouldn't have to be a beginner in front of anyone." Rogan spat a cherry pit into the yard and said, "That's the most Rose sentence I've ever heard." Rose laughed, which exonerated her a little in her own eyes, or at least shortened her sentence.

She played the open strings again that evening, alone, E A D G B E, listening to how each one was its own note and how together they made a kind of ladder she couldn't yet climb. Her grandfather had never taught her anything directly; his whole influence on her had been this putative inheritance sitting unopened in a closet, a maybe that she had finally made into a thing. She didn't know whether that counted as knowing him or just knowing his guitar. She put her fingers clumsily on the frets, trying the shape Mr. Müller had sketched for her on a napkin before he left, and plucked each string one at a time to see which ones buzzed.

Her mother passed through on her way to the kitchen and stopped, and Rose looked up with her hand still pressed against the strings. "Do you want me to keep going?" she asked.

activity: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
knowledge_domain: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
fact: In West Virginia v. Barnette (1943), the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 that public schools cannot force students to salute the flag or recite the Pledge of Allegiance.
story:
The marble stairs of city hall were worn in the middle, dished by decades of shoes, and Samuel climbed them with his outline folded into quarters in his pocket. He had drawn the petitioner's side of the case first, the side he believed, and then the respondent's, the side he had been assigned, and the two outlines had begun to metastasize into each other in his notebook until he could no longer tell which argument had been born where.

The mock court met in a committee room on the second floor, long table, bad fluorescent light, a portrait of a former mayor whose name nobody remembered. Ms. Çelik had arranged the room so the judges sat at one end and the arguing students stood, which was meant to replicate the feel of an actual bench. Samuel's case concerned a student suspended for refusing to stand during a morning announcement, and the question was whether the school could compel that kind of speech at all.

"You're petitioner again tonight," Max said, spreading his own notes across the table. "Then you flip. That's the whole exercise. Ms. Çelik wants us able to argue either side without gagging."

"That seems like it teaches you to believe nothing," Ethan said. He said it blithely, the way he said most things, as though conviction were a hobby other people took too seriously. Samuel noticed he did not entirely disagree, and that bothered him more than the remark itself.

When the round began, Samuel argued that the school had a legitimate interest in civic ritual, that standing was a small cost paid for a shared public life, and he heard himself say it so smoothly that he frightened himself a little. Then Max stood for the student and said, "In West Virginia v. Barnette, in 1943, the Supreme Court ruled six to three that public schools cannot force students to salute the flag or recite the Pledge of Allegiance." He said it plainly, without triumph, and let it sit in the room. Samuel had not found that case in his research. He wrote the citation on his pad, pressing hard enough to score the next page.

Ms. Çelik called a recess before the flip, which was unusual, and stood by the window looking down at the parking lot while the students ate vending machine crackers. Samuel went and stood near her without asking anything, and after a while she said, "Barnette gets cited every time this comes up. Every time. You might wonder why your outlines didn't find it." Then she walked back to the table, and Samuel understood that the omission had been the assignment, or part of one, though she had never said so.

For the second round he had to argue the student's side, the side he had believed all along, and found it harder than the first. The case Max had named gave him a spine for the argument, but arguing it felt different now, because he had spent forty minutes building the other one and the other one had not been stupid. He stumbled once, recovered, and asked the panel a question instead of answering theirs: "If we can't be made to salute the flag, per Barnette, six to three, 1943, is there anything the school can still ask of us in common?" One of the student judges looked at his notes and did not answer, and Samuel thought the silence was the honest reply.

Afterward the three of them sat on the steps outside city hall while the streetlights came on along the avenue. Max said Samuel's first round had been better than his second, and Ethan agreed, and Samuel found he was not sure whether they were right or whether the second round had simply been true in a way that made it uglier to listen to. He still had both outlines, folded together in his pocket, and he did not take them out to check which one he trusted.

"Same case next week," Max said, standing, brushing cracker crumbs off his jeans. "You'll get Barnette into your own brief by then?"

Samuel looked up at the lit windows of the committee room, where Ms. Çelik was stacking chairs alone. "Maybe both briefs," he said. "Maybe it belongs in both."

activity: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
knowledge_domain: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
fact: In Tinker v. Des Moines (1969), the Supreme Court ruled 7-2 that students do not shed their constitutional rights to freedom of speech at the schoolhouse gate.
story:
Justin had the living room to himself until six, which gave him three hours to believe in something he did not actually believe. The assignment from Mr. Fitzgerald was to argue both sides of a mock Supreme Court case about free speech, petitioner and respondent, five minutes each, and Justin had drawn a school dress-code dispute in which a sophomore was suspended for wearing a shirt the principal called disruptive. He spread the briefs across the coffee table, his mother's old law-school highlighters bleeding orange and green across the margins, and tried to imagine how it would feel to stand in front of the class and defend a principal who suspended a kid over a shirt.

He had almost given up when Jaidyn came through the back door without knocking, holding a bag of chips and a printed article. "Anaelle says you're doing the dress-code thing," Jaidyn said, dropping onto the couch. "She also says you looked like a funeral guest in class today."

"I'm trying to cogitate," Justin said, and immediately regretted the verb, because Jaidyn repeated it twice, savoring it like the chips.

"Cogitate all you want. You still need the famous line." Jaidyn slid the article across the table. "Here. This is the one everyone uses."

Justin read it and felt the floor tilt slightly. Tinker v. Des Moines, 1969. The Supreme Court had ruled seven to two, and the line itself was better than anything he could have written: "Students do not shed their constitutional rights to freedom of speech at the schoolhouse gate." He said it out loud twice, just to hear the rhythm of it, and the rhythm was the problem. It was so good it made his side feel pre-decided, as if the whole case were a formality. "So the student wins," he said. "Black armbands against the Vietnam War, and the Court said the school couldn't punish them. That's basically my case."

"That's one side," Jaidyn said, mouth full. "Fitzgerald made you argue both, right? That's the whole evil point of the assignment."

Justin sat with that. His first instinct had been to treat the second side as a chore, a pantomime he would perform badly on purpose, the way he had once argued in ninth grade that homework should be abolished and lost so thoroughly that even he had voted against himself. But somewhere between the highlighters and Jaidyn's chips, he started assembling the other argument for real: schools were not public squares, minors were compulsory attendees, a principal had to keep five hundred teenagers from turning the hallway into a billboard war. The reasoning had its own logos, its own clean architecture, and building it felt uncomfortably like believing it.

He tested both drafts out loud while Jaidyn pretended to be a justice, which mostly meant saying "Counselor" in a grandiose voice and interrupting with questions about lunch. When Justin argued for the student, Jaidyn nodded along. When Justin argued for the school, Jaidyn stopped chewing. "Okay, that was actually convincing," Jaidyn said. "Which is creepy. Which one do you believe?"

"I don't know," Justin said, and was surprised to find that the answer felt honest rather than lazy. He believed the schoolhouse-gate line, believed it in his chest, and he also believed that a first-period classroom was not a street corner, and the two beliefs sat side by side without shaking hands. The Court itself had split, seven to two, which meant two grown justices had looked at the same facts and landed elsewhere. That did not tell him who was right. It told him the question was real.

At six his mother came home, kissed his head without asking what he was doing because she could see he was doing it, and started dinner. Anaelle texted: still on for tomorrow? bring the tinker quote, fitzgerald loves it. Justin typed yes, then deleted it, then typed yes again, because Fitzgerald did love it, everyone loved it, and Justin had started to wonder whether loving the line was the same as understanding it.

He stacked the briefs, petitioner on top, then flipped the stack so the school's side faced up. Tomorrow he would stand in a classroom arranged like a courtroom and argue a kid's right to wear a shirt, then, ninety seconds later, argue that the shirt could wait until the sidewalk. He would probably win one side and lose the other, and he would not know until afterward which loss he minded.

From the kitchen his mother called that dinner was in ten minutes. Jaidyn stole one last chip and said, "For the record, I'm ruling for the shirt." Justin slid the article into his folder, between the two halves of himself, and said, "Objection noted."

activity: how a bill becomes a law through drafting, committee review, debate, votes and assent
knowledge_domain: how a bill becomes a law through drafting, committee review, debate, votes and assent
fact: When the US House and Senate pass different versions of a bill, a conference committee of members from both chambers can write a compromise, which both chambers must then pass.
story:
The meeting notice had been taped to the library door with the kind of tape that took paint off when you removed it, and Brooklyn read it twice before she let herself believe it. The student councils of Northgate and Riverside, the two campuses of her newly merged district, had each passed a phone policy, and the policies disagreed. Northgate's version allowed phones at lunch. Riverside's banned them from the moment a student walked through the gates. The principal had refused to sign either one until the councils produced a single text, and she had given them until Friday.

"They expect us to do this in the library," Norman said, dropping his bag on the table by the windows. "Like we're going to become reasonable near books."

"Be quiet," said the woman at the next table, without looking up.

"That's a preview of Riverside's policy," Erik said. "Their whole school is that woman."

Brooklyn unrolled the two drafts side by side. The Northgate bill had been written in a single late night by their drafting committee, five people and one box of crackers, and it read like it: clause three contradicted clause seven, and somebody had left the word "obviously" in the middle of a sentence about hallways. The Riverside bill was clean, numbered, and stricter than a monastery. She had been elected to sort this out, though nobody had explained how.

Mr. Hamdan came by with the cart of returns and stopped, reading over her shoulder. "Ah," he said. "The phone wars."

"You have an opinion?"

"I have a checkout desk forty feet from the lunch room." He shelved a book about constitutional law, spine out, and pushed it an inch flush with its neighbors. "The noise was deleterious to anyone trying to read. Look it up if you don't believe me."

"I know what it means," Brooklyn said, and he went on with the cart.

The first hour was pure collision. Norman wanted lunch phones, all lunch, every lunch. Erik wanted what he called clean halls, and when Brooklyn asked what that meant he said, "You know, clean," which she did not flag as an epistemology problem out loud, though she thought it. They traded amendments back and forth, each one struck down on a voice vote of two to one, until she realized the votes weren't the problem. The problem was that they had no procedure at all, no way to turn two bills into one.

"What did the actual government do?" she asked no one, and then answered herself by pulling the book Mr. Hamdan had shelved. She read with her finger under the line. When the House and Senate pass different versions of a bill, a conference committee, made up of members from both chambers, can write a compromise, which both chambers must then pass. Not the president. Not the principal. Both chambers, or nothing.

She read it aloud once, quietly, then again.

"So we pick a few people from each council," Norman said.

"And whatever we write, both councils have to pass it," Erik said. "Not just agree to it. Vote on it."

"And Ms. Reyes is the assent," Brooklyn said. "She signs at the end. Like the president." She was already tearing a page from her notebook. "Three from each side. That's the committee."

Riverside sent three delegates to the library on Thursday, and the committee argued for two hours in the biography section, which Brooklyn chose because it felt appropriate. The Riverside delegation was led by a girl who spoke in complete paragraphs and treated every concession as a hostage exchange. Phones at lunch, yes, but not in hallways. Hallways, yes, but not during passing periods, which Norman pointed out were hallways. The girl wanted a study-hall ban added. Norman called that deleterious, clearly showing off, and she said, "Now you're just using words."

"The word is fine," Brooklyn said. "The timing's rude."

By Friday morning they had a text: phones permitted at lunch and in study halls, banned during class and passing periods, enforcement by teachers rather than a new bureaucracy, review after one semester. It was nobody's first choice, which Brooklyn had begun to suspect was the definition of a compromise. The Northgate council debated it for forty minutes, mostly about the word "bureaucracy," and passed it. The Riverside council debated it for fifty-five minutes, mostly about whether a semester was long enough to prove anything, and passed it by two votes.

She carried the single copy to the office herself. Ms. Reyes read it at the counter, pen already uncapped, and Brooklyn watched her hesitate over the last line, the review clause, the part that admitted they might have gotten it wrong. The pen went down on the paper.

"One semester," Ms. Reyes said, signing. "Set a reminder."

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
knowledge_domain: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
fact: Compound or coating chocolate, which replaces some or all cocoa butter with other fats, sets without tempering but does not have the same snap.
story:
Florence had been peeling garlic for Ms. Liu for two summers before she was allowed near the chocolate, and now, on the third Saturday of September, she stood at the back of the market stall watching a silver bowl of melted couverture cool against her wrist. The farmers' market ran along the river until one in the afternoon, and by ten the smell of warm cocoa drifted past the honey vendor and the man who sold nothing but nine kinds of tomato. Ms. Liu sold handmade bars and dipped figs, and she taught by adjacency rather than instruction. "Stir," she said, "and watch the thermometer, not the clock." Florence stirred. The chocolate moved from glossy and loose to something thicker, and her arm ached in a way that felt earned.

Keanna arrived at eleven with a paper cup of cider and her elbows already sunburned from the campsite where she'd spent the weekend. She leaned on the stall's edge and told them about making s'mores, and then about something stranger: she had brought candy melts for her little cousins, melted them in a tin pot over the fire, and dipped strawberries that had hardened perfectly in the shade within minutes, shiny as lacquer, no thermometer anywhere. "So what's all this?" she asked, nodding at Florence's thermometer, its line creeping down through twenty-nine degrees. "Why do you need that thing when mine just set on their own?"

Florence opened her mouth and found she didn't know, and Ms. Liu, who never answered a question she thought a person could answer herself, went to make change for a customer. Charles-Antoine, who had biked over from his shift at the library, said maybe the melts had a chemical in them, which sounded to Florence like the kind of answer that exculpated the person giving it, since it explained nothing while sounding like something. He shrugged when she said so. Keanna said she'd read the package on the drive home; the words had been "compound" something. "Compound chocolate," Florence repeated, and then, because Ms. Liu's boxes were stacked within arm's reach, she pulled one down and turned it over, and there on the label was the phrase she half-remembered from the flyer in Ms. Liu's kitchen: compound or coating chocolate, which replaces some or all of the cocoa butter with other fats.

"It sets without tempering," she read aloud, "but it does not have the same snap." Keanna looked doubtful, as though Florence had recited a spell in a language neither of them trusted, so Ms. Liu, returning with an empty fig tray, broke one of Keanna's own strawberries, which she had brought in a container in her backpack, gods of the campsite willing, and snapped one of her own bars beside it. Keanna's berry broke with a soft, bending give, like a candle. Ms. Liu's bar cracked clean, a sound like a knuckle, and the broken face shone. "Different fats," Ms. Liu said, and would say no more, which was her way of saying the rest was Florence's to figure out.

The rest, Florence was beginning to understand, was the whole afternoon. She stirred and cooled and reheated, chasing the narrow window where the chocolate would set shiny, and twice she blew it. The first batch seized into a dull, grainy paste when she let it drop too far, and Ms. Liu scraped it back into the melting pot without ceremony, as though failure were simply an ingredient that had gone in early. The second batch bloomed with pale streaks as it set on the marble slab, and Florence thought of her mother telling her, all through her applications last spring, that anything worth doing could be done quickly if you were smart enough, and how much she had wanted that to be true, and how the marble kept saying otherwise, slowly, in a language of streaks and cracks.

Charles-Antoine called her sagacious when she diagnosed her own mistake, a too-fast pour, but he said it in the mocking way he used for words he'd found in the thesaurus that morning, so it landed somewhere between compliment and travesty. She took it as both. He had watched her rewrite her college essay nine times in August, cutting every phrase she loved, and he alone knew what that had cost, and so he alone knew what it meant when she stood at the slab and said, quietly, that maybe the essay had been wrong of her to keep, or maybe she'd cut it badly, the way you could ruin chocolate by cooling it in the wrong direction, and she genuinely did not know which. He didn't answer. He ate a seized batch that Ms. Liu had rolled into truffle-sized lumps and pronounced it better than the good stuff, which it was not, but Florence loved him for it.

By half past twelve she had a bowl that behaved, that poured in a ribbon with a satin sheen, that set on the figs with the clean, glassy face she'd been chasing since June. Ms. Liu handed her a box of them for the road and took no money, which was her way of marking an occasion without naming one. Keanna, gathering her backpack, said she'd stick to her candy melts forever, since they asked nothing of her and gave her shiny strawberries at a campfire, and Florence found she couldn't argue, because Keanna was not wrong, only different, and the difference was the whole point.

They were stacking the tables when a woman in a linen dress bought the last two bars of Ms. Liu's, cracked one immediately on the counter to hear the snap, and then, holding the pieces up to the light, asked whether they were made with real cocoa butter or with one of those compound coatings, since she was avoiding the real thing on her doctor's advice, and only wanted the fake. Ms. Liu looked at Florence. Florence handed the woman the last of Keanna's strawberries.

activity: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
knowledge_domain: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
fact: In periodized training, a season is divided into cycles; a microcycle, the smallest, usually lasts about one week.
story:
The clipboard had belonged to Samuel's father, a plastic thing with a crack across one corner, and on it Samuel had written seven days in his smallest handwriting. Monday, skills. Tuesday, conditioning. Wednesday, skills. Thursday, conditioning. Friday, skills. Saturday, game. Sunday, more conditioning, because Sunday had always felt like a day he was wasting.

"You look like you're doing our taxes," Hugo said, dropping onto the bench beside him at the edge of the soccer field. The afternoon practice had ended, the nets were still up, and a groundskeeper was walking the far touchline picking up cones.

"I'm building a training program. For the whole season." Samuel turned the clipboard so Hugo could see. "Coach said whoever plans their own week gets to captain the Sunday sessions."

Hugo squinted at it. "There's no rest anywhere. You've got yourself doing something every single day."

"Rest is for people who aren't serious."

"Rest is for people whose legs work," Hugo said. "You watched Violette at Saturday's game? She sat out the second half with her calf wrapped."

Samuel had watched. Violette was the fastest player in their year, and watching her limp to the sideline had been like watching a machine develop a fault no one could locate. He turned the clipboard back toward himself and looked at Sunday again.

He found her by the equipment shed, sitting on a stack of folded pinnies with an ice bag balanced on her leg. Violette was not a virtuoso in the way people used the word at school, all flash and no foundation; her game was cerebral, built on angles and patience, and she rarely spoke about any of it.

"Did you train every day before the injury?" Samuel asked.

"Every day since I was eleven." She adjusted the ice bag. "My old coach kept telling me to stop. I didn't."

"So what went wrong?"

"That's the thing, nothing went wrong. No tackle, no twist. The physio said my calf just gave out. Overuse. Which is a very polite way of saying I did this to myself." She looked at his clipboard. "What's that?"

"My program." He handed it over, and she read it without expression, which was worse than laughing.

"You're going to be me in about eight weeks," she said.

That evening Samuel's father was at the kitchen table with his laptop, and Samuel sat across from him and asked whether an engine could fail from being run too well. His father considered the question long enough that Samuel regretted it, then said only, "Look it up properly. Don't guess."

In his room, with the clipboard on his knees, Samuel searched. Most of what he found was forums, people arguing about supplements, but one coaching manual had a whole chapter on periodized training. It said a season was divided into cycles, and that the smallest of these, the microcycle, usually lasted about one week. He read the sentence three times. His own program was not a season divided into anything; it was a wall with no mortar, days pressed against days.

He brought the manual to school and cornered Hugo before class. "It has a name. A microcycle. A week, basically. That's the unit you build from."

"Congratulations," Hugo said. "You've invented Monday."

But at practice that afternoon, Ms. Sutherland, who coached the senior team and had volunteered to look at the captains' plans, stopped at Samuel's clipboard for a long moment. The new version had rest written into Sunday and a warm-up block at the top of every session, and it was shorter than everyone else's, visibly shorter, and Samuel could feel the others deciding he had done less work.

"Who taught you this?" Ms. Sutherland asked.

"A book. And Violette's leg."

She nodded once and moved on to the next clipboard, which belonged to a boy named Dev from another class, a dense seven-day wall of drills that went unchanged from Monday to Sunday. Ms. Sutherland praised Dev's commitment in front of the group. She said it was exactly the kind of dedication she liked to see, and Dev stood a little taller, and Samuel said nothing, because arguing would have sounded like excusing his own thin page.

On Sunday morning Samuel arrived early to run his session, cones laid out, warm-up ladder set, the whole microcycle mapped for the week ahead: two hard days, one easy, one rest, a game at the end. The field was quiet and slightly damp. At nine o'clock exactly, Dev arrived, alone, in full kit, carrying a stopwatch.

"Ms. Sutherland said the committed players could do extras," Dev said, and began setting up his own cones on the other half of the field, "before your session. Since yours starts with, you know." He glanced at the ladder, at the slow deliberate footwork Samuel was demonstrating. "Walking."

"Static stretching," said Dev, and jogged off toward the far goal, stopwatch clicking, before Samuel could say a word.

activity: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
knowledge_domain: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
fact: The Haymarket affair in Chicago on May 4, 1886, grew out of protests for an eight-hour workday and is considered the origin of May 1 as International Workers' Day.
story:
Colton set his phone face-down beside his plate, which was a gesture of discipline he immediately regretted, because the letter was due to Amar by Friday and it was already Thursday dinner. The letter was Amar's idea: a signed list of the grocery store's part-time workers asking for breaks that actually happened and schedules posted more than two days in advance. Six names so far. Colton had five.

His father ladled stew into Mr. Clarke's bowl before his own, because Mr. Clarke had come over to return the ladder and stayed, as he always did, for the smell of onions. "Colton's got some labor dispute brewing," his father said. "Tell him he's sixteen. Tell him he should be grateful he has a job at all."

"I'm not ungrateful," Colton said. "I'm tired. Thursday I closed until eleven on a school night, and Friday he does it again, and the schedule went up Tuesday." He could feel his own voice getting away from him. "There's a meeting at the store Saturday. Whatever we hand in before then is what the manager sees."

Mr. Clarke chewed slowly, the way he did everything. "When I was your age I walked a picket line with my mother," he said, and then said nothing else about it, which was typical, a door opened an inch and held.

Colton's father began to gesticulate with his spoon, sweeping it across the table as though clearing away an argument no one had made yet. "Unions," he said, as if the word itself were the whole case against them. "You know what happens. Fees, politics, the whole thing turns into another kind of plutocracy, just a different set of people at the top."

"That's actually not what plutocracy means," Colton said. "It means rule by the wealthy. If it's a different set of people at the top, that's just... a different oligarchy, I guess." His father's spoon paused midair. Gabriella had drilled him on the word for the vocabulary quiz last month, quizzing him in the bleachers while the field hockey team ran laps, and he was privately glad something from that afternoon had survived.

"Fine," his father said. "Whatever it's called. The point is you quit if you don't like it."

"And then next kid gets the eleven o'clock shifts."

The screen door banged and Amar came in without knocking, holding a stack of printed pages, his draft of the letter with the six signatures. He dropped into the chair beside Colton, took a bowl without being offered, because in this house that was how it worked. "Gabriella's mom said her factory used to have a union contract," he said. "Hours, breaks, all of it written down. They couldn't just change your schedule because they felt like it. She said there are laws now, too, about how late minors can work on school nights."

"Then the manager is already breaking the law," Colton's father said, quieter now, and Colton watched something inchoate move across his father's face, not quite an opinion forming, more like the place where one might form.

Colton turned his phone over. He had been researching at lunch, in the library, while Gabriella kept watch for the hall monitor, and he had screenshots. "Look at this," he said, and read aloud, slow, so Amar could hear over his stew. "The Haymarket affair in Chicago, May 4, 1886. It grew out of protests for an eight-hour workday. It's considered the origin of May 1 as International Workers' Day." He set the phone down between the salt and the bread. "Workers march on May first in, like, most countries in the world. I always thought it was some communist thing we just didn't do. It's because of that."

"Because of Chicago," Mr. Clarke said, and touched his bowl with one finger, as if checking it was real. "My mother marched on May first every year she lived in this country. She never told me why. I figured it was just something she brought with her."

Nobody said anything for a moment. The radiator ticked. Colton's father put down his spoon.

"So we're asking for posted schedules and real breaks," Amar said. "Not eight hours. I mean, we work four-hour shifts."

"I know it's not the same thing," Colton said. "I'm not saying we're those people. I'm saying somebody wrote down what they wanted, too, and it started as something small, like this, and it took eighty years to get the eight-hour day, and maybe that's the pace of it. Or maybe I'm romanticizing. I honestly can't tell." He looked at the letter, at the six signatures, one of which was Mr. Delgado from produce, signed in careful cursive. "I keep going back and forth on whether we're doing something or just doing something."

"You're doing it either way," Mr. Clarke said.

Colton picked up the pen from beside Amar's pages and signed under the sixth name, the seventh line, his handwriting smaller than he expected. Then he pushed the letter across the table toward his father, who looked at it for a long moment, picked up the pen, and wrote his own name in the margin beside it, and dated it Thursday.

activity: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
knowledge_domain: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
fact: The 1947 Taft-Hartley Act, passed over President Truman's veto, allowed US states to pass right-to-work laws banning contracts that require workers to pay union fees.
story:
Sophia slid her name tag across the table so her mother could read it, S-A-P-P-H-O as the break room manager had printed it, and waited for the usual joke. Her mother only said the soup was getting cold.

"That's not how you spell it," her father said, not looking up from his plate.

"It's how he transliterated it from the application form. I wrote it in English letters, he typed in what he saw." Sophia pulled the tag back. "Corbin did it. He's been there since June."

Her father set down his fork. "Corbin. He's the one from Ohio?"

"Michigan." She had mentioned the two of them at dinner before, how Corbin trained her on the scanner and Cierra covered her break when the line backed up, but tonight there was something else, and she had been rehearsing how to bring it up since the bus. "They had an argument today. About the union."

Her mother's hands went still around the ladle. Her father worked at the plant across the river, and the word union in their kitchen was like the name of a relative nobody had spoken to in years.

"The contract says everyone pays dues," Sophia said. "Twenty-something dollars a paycheck. Corbin says he's not paying, because where he's from in Michigan he never had to. Cierra says he has to here, because she's from New Mexico and she always has. And the steward just told them to sort it out with the local office, which nobody has time to do." She took a breath. "I looked it up on my phone during break."

"And?" her father said.

"And there's this thing called right-to-work. States can pass laws that ban contracts requiring workers to pay union fees. It comes from the Taft-Hartley Act. Nineteen forty-seven. Congress passed it over President Truman's veto, which I didn't even know was possible, a law surviving a veto, but it is, if enough of them vote for it." She was speaking too fast and slowed down. "Our state doesn't have a right-to-work law. So here, the contract can require the fees, and Corbin has to pay. In his state, it couldn't."

The synchronicity of it had struck her on the bus, that she and Corbin and Cierra had all turned eighteen within months of each other and landed at the same loading dock with three different sets of rules in their heads, none of which they had chosen. She didn't say that part out loud. At the table it would have sounded like a speech.

"So he owes money," her father said.

"He thinks he doesn't. And honestly, at first I thought Cierra was right just because she sounded sure. But being sure isn't the same as being from a state where the law's different." She had gone back and reread the summary twice, once on the bus and once walking up the street, because the first read made it seem like Corbin was freeloading and the second made it seem like the union was forcing him, and neither framing felt tenable once she could actually picture the two of them, Corbin holding his checkstub, Cierra holding hers, identical except for one deduction neither of them understood.

"Which one's right?" her mother asked.

"Legally, Cierra. Morally, I don't know. Corbin gets the same raise she does, the same break schedule, the same everything the union negotiated, whether he pays or not. That's what makes him angry, paying for a thing he'd get free. And that's what makes her angry, carrying it for him." Sophia pushed a potato around her plate. "I told him tomorrow I'd go with him to the union hall at lunch. Not to argue. Just so somebody tells him the actual rule out loud, from the source, instead of us guessing."

Her father was quiet for a while. "When I started at the plant, a man named Delgado sat me down the first week and told me which dues were worth it and which grievances weren't. Nobody made him do that."

"That's the thing, though. You chose to stay in. Corbin's never gotten to choose anything. He moved here in March because his uncle said the warehouse was hiring."

"He can choose now," her father said. "Pay or don't, but do it knowing what the law is. That's more than most people get."

Her mother refilled his bowl without asking. Sophia folded her napkin and put it beside her plate, then took it back and put it on her lap, because she wasn't finished eating, because tomorrow was decided and the soup was still warm.

"Can I borrow the car at noon?" she asked. "The union hall is two buses away."

Her father reached into his pocket for the keys and set them next to the salt.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: In 1977 Tuckman and Mary Ann Jensen added a fifth stage, adjourning, for when a group's work ends and members separate.
story:
The last game of the season ended 3-1, and the other team's families carried coolers across the field like a small parade. Nathan stood in the goalmouth where he had spent the whole autumn, the grass there worn to mud in the shape of his own small movements, and he understood that he would never stand there again. Next year, if he made the college team, it would be a different net, different hands slapping his shoulders, a coach whose face he could not yet imagine.

The end-of-season party was in Kessler Park, under the pavilion by the duck pond. Nathan arrived early with his mother's folding chairs and found Mr. Greco already there, taping a paper banner that read WAYLAND SOCCER, FALL SEASON. Mr. Greco taught sophomore English and coached the team on evenings and Saturdays, and he had a way of assigning homework even to people who weren't in his class. "Nathan," he called down from the stepladder, "you're the one taking psych, yes? Tell me if this is straight." He held up the banner and waited, and Nathan said it was, though the right corner sagged.

Mitchell came next, still in his warmup jacket though the game had been over for an hour, carrying a grocery bag of sodas he had clearly bought himself. Then Reese, who had scored the single goal they'd managed, her hair still wet from the showers. The seniors gathered around the picnic table closest to the pond: Nathan, Mitchell, Reese, and two others who drifted in with paper plates. It was a small archipelago of people, Nathan thought, each on their own little island of plans. Mitchell had a scholarship interview in January. Reese was going halfway across the country. Nathan had a dorm assignment and a roommate he had spoken to twice, both times about a mini fridge.

He had learned the Tuckman thing in September, in the first week of psychology, half listening because the season had just started and his mind was on cleats and lineups. The teacher had put up a slide about groups. Nathan remembered copying it down without interest. Now, at the table, while Mitchell argued with Reese about whether the second goal had been offside, the memory surfaced with a kind of visceral force, the way you suddenly feel a bruise you got days ago.

"Wait," Nathan said. "Hang on. Listen." They didn't hang on, so he said it louder. "In 1977 Tuckman and Mary Ann Jensen added a fifth stage. It's called adjourning. For when a group's work ends and members separate."

Mitchell set down his soda. "You're doing homework at a party."

"I'm not doing homework." But he was, in a way, and he couldn't stop. He told them what he remembered: that a psychologist named Tuckman had described the stages groups go through, that for years there were four, and that in 1977 he and a researcher named Mary Ann Jensen had looked at all of it again and added one more, the last one, the one for endings. He said it haltingly, checking each piece against his notes in memory, afraid of getting it wrong in front of Reese, who was the kind of person who looked things up.

She already had her phone out. "Nineteen seventy-seven," she confirmed. "Bruce Tuckman and Mary Ann Jensen. Adjourning." She turned the screen toward him, and there it was, the same diagram that had captivated nobody in September and now seemed to be about the exact table they were sitting at.

"So what are the other four?" Mitchell asked, reaching for her phone.

"Forming, storming, norming, performing," Nathan said, and found he could say them in order, like a rhyme he'd learned without knowing he'd learned it. "That's not the point, though. The point is that for a long time people thought the story ended with the group working. Doing the thing. Performing." He gestured at the field beyond the pavilion, where the goals still stood with their nets sagging. "Nobody thought the ending was a stage. It was just, you know, after. And then these two said no, it counts too. When the work ends and everyone separates, that's part of it. It has a name."

Mr. Greco had come down off the ladder at some point and was sitting at the next table with his tape and his coffee, and Nathan was glad to see that he did not say anything. He just listened, the way he listened when a student found something out on their own.

For a while nobody spoke. Down at the pond a child was throwing bread to the ducks with more enthusiasm than aim, and the light was doing that thing it did in November, going gold and then gray within a quarter hour. Nathan thought about how he had spent the season wanting things: to start, to win, to be seen by the college scout who had come once in October and sat in a folding chair and written nothing, as far as Nathan could tell, the whole second half. He had wanted the season to matter in a way he could carry with him, and here at the end it seemed the wanting and the having were not the same shape. What he would carry was smaller and stranger: Mitchell's terrible halftime jokes, Reese learning everyone's warmup songs, the mud print of his own feet in the goalmouth. Maybe the having was that.

"So it's not just over," Reese said. "It's adjourning."

"Technically we're adjourning right now," Mitchell said, and raised his soda can, and the two others at the table raised their paper cups even though they had missed the beginning of the conversation entirely. Nathan lifted his can too. He didn't know yet whether the five of them would still be texting in March, whether Reese would answer when he wrote from her new city, whether any of it would hold its shape at a distance. Adjourning, as far as he could tell, didn't promise that. It only said this part was real and deserved a name, and Nathan found he believed it, and that believing it was not the same as being ready.

Mr. Greco folded his stepladder as the sky went gray. "Help me with the nets before it's dark," he said, and the seniors got up together, all six of them, and walked out onto the field.
